case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 12th day of July, 2000 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 1086 of 1968.)
full_judgment:
Md Muzammel Hossain CJ: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my brothers, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J. and Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the reasoning and findings given by Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J.

Surendra Kumar Sinha J: I agree with my learned brother Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. that this appeal should be dismissed, but I feel tempted to express my opinion separately on taking into consideration the laws involved in this appeal which are of public importance on the prevailing land laws. The questions involved in this appeal are whether, the transaction between the predecessors of the parties was alive on the date of promulgation of the President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 (PO 88 of 1972), and whether, the suit for redemption of mortgage is maintainable as the transaction being past and closed one. The determination of these questions require the construction of the deed dated 22nd April, 1926, Exhibit-1, executed by Anwarul Ali and 4 others, the predecessors of the plaintiffs in favour of Omra Khatun Chowdhury, the predecessor of the defendants which transaction is a mortgage by conditional sale or a sale with a condition to repurchase within the meaning of section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

3. If the transaction is a mortgage by conditional sale, the suit instituted by the plaintiffs for redemption of mortgage is maintainable as being not barred by limitation and if it is found that the transaction is a sale with a condition to repurchase or it is past and closed one, the suit will be dismissed on the ground of limitation. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit is maintainable but the lower appellate court reversed the judgment of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The High Court Division on consideration of the deed and the cases of Bangladesh vs Hazi Abdul Gani Biswas, 32 DLR (AD) 233, Abu Bakkar vs Nazir Ahmed, 34 DLR (AD) 237, Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat vs Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat, 1 BLC (AD) 94 and Anwaruddin Bepari vs Assistant Commissioner, 1 BLC (AD) 164, came to the conclusion that the transaction is a mortgage by conditional sale and held that the suit is not barred by limitation. It restored the decree of the trial Court.

4. In the prefix of the deed, it was described as mortgage deed for a period of five years and the price for this period of transfer was fixed at Taka 1,000 stipulating that if the vendors could repay the said amount in the month of Chaitra within this period of 5 years from the date of its execution, Omra Khatun Chowdhury would handover possession in favour of Anwarul Ali and others, the predecessors of the plaintiffs. But if they failed to repay the said amount, they would be entitled to recover possession through the process of court treating it as foreclosed deed.

5. It is argued on behalf of the appellant that the transaction is not a mortgage by conditional sale but it is an out and out sale and that the transaction is past and closed one and thus, the suit is barred by limitation. On the other hand, it is argued on behalf of the respondents that the transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale and the period of limitation for redemption of the land is sixty years and that the suit is not barred by limitation.

6. In resolving the question in controversy, there are inconsistent findings both by the Court of appeal below and the High Court Division. The Courts including the High Court Division are confused in deciding the point in controversy in the light of section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and sections 95 and 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. It is pertinent at this juncture to consider the meaning of the word ''mortgage'' defined in section 58 of the Transfer of the Property Act which means:

"The transfer of an interest in specific immovable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability".

7. There are different kinds of mortgages of them we are concerned with ''mortgage by conditional sale within the meaning of section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, which provides; "where the mortgagor ostensibly sells the mortgaged property—

"On condition that on default of payment of the mortgage money on a certain date the sale shall become absolute, or

On condition that on such payment being made the sale shall become void, or

On condition that on such payment being made the buyer shall transfer the property to the seller.

the transaction is called a mortgage by conditional sale and the mortgagee a mortgagee by conditional sale.

Provided that no such transaction shall be deemed to be a mortgage, unless the condition is embodied in the document which effects or purports to effect the sale".

8. This proviso was inserted by the Transfer of Property (Amendment) Act, 1929. The earliest traces of the law of mortgage can be found in the Roman Law of mancipitio contracta fiducia, i.e. a sale with a contract or agreement for redemption; or in other words, it was an actual conveyance of property upon an agreement that if the purchase money were repaid, the lender would reconvey the property to the borrower. The word ''fiducia'' means a conditional conveyance under which the property whatever its value was forfeited in case of non payment. This was followed by ‘pignus’ which was a transfer not of ownership but of possession without liability to forfeiture. Then the stage is the ''hypotheca'', a form of pledge without delivery of possession under which the creditor acquired a power. But this was not a convenient form of mortgage, because, if the lender sold away the property the borrower could not follow it in the hands of the purchaser; so, in time, the simple form of ‘pignus’  came to supersede it. While the ''Fiducia'' gave the lender both possession and ownership, ‘pignus’ gave him only possession leaving ownership with the borrower. A further improvement was achieved in the ''Hypotheca'' which retained both possession and ownership with the debtor giving the creditor a real right in the nature of servitude over the property. Ultimately the power of sale was conferred on the pledge, and thus the property became a security for his money. Here we have noticed three distinct stages in the history of Roman mortgage law ''Fiducia'', ‘pignus’  and ''Hypotheca'' with the power of sale.

9. In England the original mortgage at common law was rather a pledge than a mortgage. The transfer was not of title, but of possession. At a later time the English mortgage took the modern form of a conditional conveyance. This condition was originally one of defeasance that on repayment the grant determined and the land reverted to the mortgagor who was entitled to re-enter. After the common law mortgage became a mortgage by conditional conveyance; it was modified by three principles of equity; such as:

a) that equity looks to the essence of the transaction and that a mortgage is essence of borrowing transaction;

b) that the borrower is in need of protection and that a condition that penalizes him is void;

c) that a condition of forfeiture in default of payment on the due date is a penalty

10. These equitable principles have been applied to the law of mortgages in the Transfer of Property Act. A mortgage is a transfer and in the next place it is a transfer of interest in specific immovable property. A mortgage may be created to secure payment of debt, whether present or future or to secure performance of an obligation which may give rise to some pecuniary liability. Thus, we find that in case of a mortgage the relationship of borrower and lender exists. For creating a mortgage it is to be seen whether the words used in the deed sufficiently indicate an intention to create a security for a debt. References in this connection arc the cases of Hunooman Prasad vs Mst. Babooee. 6 MIA 393 and Rajkumar vs Ramdutt. 5 BLR 264 (FB). If this intention is absent, the transaction will be not a mortgage, although it is described as such. On the other hand, if the intention is to create a security for a debt, it will be a mortgage by whatever name it may be called. In cases where the intention of the parties has been ambiguously expressed, the nomenclature of the deed may be a useful guide for determining the nature of the transaction.

11. In a mortgage by conditional sale, the ostensible sale is conditional and intended as security for the debt. In case of payment on the date fixed the condition was that the sale became void. Though a transaction of ''sale with a condition of retransfer'' has not been mentioned in section 58 of the Transfer of property Act, the English Courts and the Privy Council on construction of section 58 and different instruments made distinction between a mortgage by conditional sale and a sale with a condition of retransfer in the context of section 58 of the Transfer of property Act. Similar type of transaction has been inserted in section 95A of Act, 1950 by president''s Order No.136 of 1972 (P0 136 of 1972) providing that such transaction be deemed to be a ''complete usufructory mortgage'' over which, I shall discuss later on. As regards ''sale with a condition of repurchase'' it is observed, it is not a mortgage, for the relationship of debtor and creditor does not subsist and there is no debt for which the transfer is a security. It is not a partial transfer, but a transfer of all rights in the property reserving only a personal right of repurchase or preemption which is lost if not exercised within the stipulated time. The above views were taken in Alderson vs White, (1858) 2 De G & J, 97 and these views were accepted by the Judicial Committee in Bhagwan Sahi vs Bhagzvan Din, (1890) 12 All 387.

12. In Bhagwan Sahi, (Supra), the case degends upon construction of two deeds dated 20 February, 1835, by the first document Alum Singh and others, professed to be the proprietors of the property mentioned that they had of their own accord absolutely sold the entire property to Ganga Din. On the same day another deed was executed by which Ganga Din said that he had purchased the property for Rs. 4,000 and added that "However, I have as a matter of favour, mercy, kindness and indulgence, executed this deed, and so hereby stipulate that if all these vendors will within a period of ten years from the date of this deed pay in a lump sum, and without interest, the whole amount specified above, I shall accept the same, and cancel this valid sale ". After 50 years of the deed the suit was filed on behalf of the vendors claiming to redeem the property on payment of the Rs.4,000. The defendant claimed that it was an absolute sale. The trial Court decreed the suit and on appeal, the Allahabad High Court affirmed the decree. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, however, reversed the finding holding that the vendors did not stipulate that they should have a right to repurchase, but the vendee, as a matter of grace and kindness, stipulated that they should have that right. Their Lordships quoted with approval the following passage in Alderson;

"The rule of law on this subject is one dictated by common sense that prima-facie an absolute conveyance containing nothing to show that the relation of debtor and creditor is to exist between the parties does not cease to be an absolute conveyance and become a mortgage merely because the vendor stipulates that he shall have a right to repurchase".

13. As to the difference in the legal effect of a sale with a condition of repurchase and a mortgage by conditional sale, it is said in some decisions, it is often a matter of extreme difficulty to decide which of these two transactions a particular document or set of documents discloses. The distinction is purely one of intention whether it was intended that the relation of debtor and creditor should subsist (Abdul Latif vs Abdul Gani, 1939 AC 730) and the question of what evidence is relevant to prove that intention. Before the Evidence Act came into force, oral evidence and other instruments were admitted to prove this intention but section 92 excludes evidence of an inconsistent oral agreement and provides only for cases of fraud invalidating a document. The Courts arc, therefore, practically limited to the document itself, and devised various criteria for determining whether the intention was to mortgage or to sell.

14. As pointed out by the Judicial Committee in "Narasingerji Gyanagerji VP Parthasaradhi, 51 IA 305: (AIR 1924 PC 226), that the circumstance that the transaction as phrased in the document is ostensibly a sale with a right of repurchase in the vendor, the appearance being laboriously maintained by the words of conveyance needlessly iterating the description of an absolute interest or the right of repurchase bearing the appearance of a right in relation to the exercise of which time was of the essence is not decisive. The question in each case is one of determination of the real character of the transaction to be ascertained from the provisions of the deed viewed in the light of surrounding circumstances. It was observed by the Judicial Committee:

If the words are plain and unambiguous they must in the light of the evidence of surrounding circumstances be given their true legal effect. If there is ambiguity in the language employed, the intention may be ascertained from the contents of the deed with such extrinsic evidence as may by law be permitted to be adduced to show in what manner the language of the deed was related to existing facts. Oral evidence of intention is not admissible in interpreting the covenants of the deed but evidence to explain or even to contradict the recitals as distinguished from the terms of the documents may of course be given. Evidence of contemporaneous conduct is always admissible as a surrounding circumstances, but evidence as to subsequent conduct of the parties is inadmissible''.

15. In a mortgage, the debt subsists and a right to redeem remains with the debtor; but a sale with a condition of repurchase is not a borrowing arrangement; no debt subsists and no right to redeem is reserved by the debtor but only a personal right to repurchase. This personal right can only be enforced strictly according to the terms of the deed and at the time agreed upon. In a mortgage by conditional sale the right of redemption subsists notwithstanding that the mortgagor has failed to pay at the time stated. By addition of a proviso to clause (c) of section 58 of the Transfer Property Act by the amending Act in 1929, the position has been resolved clearly. The effect of the proviso is that if the condition for repurchase is not embodied in the document which effects or purports to effect a sale, the transaction will not be regarded as a mortgage. It comes that a transaction in which the stipulation for repurchase is contained in a separate document cannot be a mortgage of any kind because it cannot fall under any other category of mortgage as per the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act. But it does not follow that if the stipulation for reconveyance is embodied in the same deed, the transaction be taken as a mortgage.

16. In Pandit Chunchun Jhn vs Sheikh Ebadat Ali, (1955) 1 SCR 174, Bose, J observed ''the legislation has made a clear cut classification and excluded transaction embodied in more than one document from the category of mortgages, therefore, it is reasonable to suppose that persons who, after the amendment, choose not to use two documents, do not intend the transaction to be a sale, unless they displace that presumption by clear and express words; and if the conditions of section 58(c) are fulfilled, then we are of opinion that the deed should be construed as a mortgage.'' This follows that where the transaction is embodied in one document and once its terms are covered by section 58(c), then there is a presumption that the transaction is a mortgage unless there are express words to indicate the contrary or in case of ambiguity, the attendant circumstances necessarily lead to the opposite conclusion.

17. Similar opinion has been expressed in a later case in Bhaskor vs Shrinarayan, AIR 1960 SC 301. In that case the deed conveys absolute title to certain properties. The transferors contended that the property transferred was intended to be mortgaged under a deed of conditional sale. The transferees contended that by the deed an absolute conveyance of the property conveyed was intended and that the conveyance was subject to a condition of repurchase to be exercised within a period of five years from the date of the deed. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground of limitation. The High Court held that the transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale and decreed the suit for redemption. Shah, J: Speaking for the Court stated that prior to the amendment there was a conflict of decisions on the question whether the condition contained in a separate deed could be taken into account in ascertaining whether a mortgage was intended the principal deed. The Legislature resolved this conflict by enacting that a transaction shall not be deemed to be a mortgage unless the condition referred to in the clause is embodied in the document which effects or purports to effect the sale. But it does not follow that if the condition is incorporated in the deed effecting or purporting to effect a sale a mortgage transaction must of necessity have been intended, Shah, J. then observed:

"The question whether by the incorporation of such a condition a transaction ostensibly of sale may be regarded as a mortgage is one of intention of the parties to be gathered from the language of the deed interpreted in the light of the surrounding circumstances. The circumstance that the condition is incorporated in the sale deed must undoubtedly be taken into account, but the value to be attached thereto must vary with the degree of formality attending upon the transaction. The definition of a mortgage by conditional sale postulates the creation by the transfer of a relation of mortgagor and the mortgagee, the price being charged on the property conveyed. In a sale coupled with an agreement to reconvey there is no relation of debtor and creditor nor is the price charged upon the property conveyed, but the sale is subject to an obligation to retransfer the property within the period specified. What distinguishes the two transactions is the relationship of debtor and creditor and the transfer being a security for the debt. The form in which the deed is clothed is not decisive. The definition of a mortgage by conditional sale itself contemplates an ostensible sale of the property".

18. It was enacted in the amendment that transaction shall not be deemed to be a mortgage unless the condition referred to the clause is embodied in the document which effects or purports to effect the sale. But it does not follow that if the condition is incorporated in the deed effecting or purporting of effect a sale, a mortgage transaction must of necessity have been intended to resolve the question it is necessary to look at the deed as a whole and the language used in the deed. The definition of ''a mortgage by conditional sale'' postulates the creation by the transfer of a relation of mortgagor and the mortgagee, the price being charged on the property conveyed. In a sale coupled with an agreement to reconvey, there is no relationship of debtor and creditor nor is the price charged upon the property conveyed but the sale is to subject an obligation to transfer the property within the period specified. The distinguishing feature of these two transactions is the relationship of debtor and creditor and the transfer being a security for debt. The definition of a mortgage by conditional sale itself contemplates an ostensible sale of the property.

19. It was argued on behalf of the appellant that the plaintiffs claim of redemption under section 95A of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act being barred, the suit is also barred as being past and closed transaction. This claim was based on a wrong premise. In ''usufructory mortgage'' defined in section 58(d), the mortgagee is placed in possession and has a right to enjoy the usufructs until the debt is paid. As possession by the mortgage is the distinguishing feature of such a mortgage; it follows that there cannot be two different usufructory mortgages on the same property at the same time. When a mortgage was executed and the property mortgaged was leased out to the mortgagee, both formed one transaction which was a usufructory mortgage and not a simple mortgage. The characteristics of a usufructory mortgage are that (a) there is no personal liability on the mortgagor, (b) no time limit is fixed, and (c) the mortgagee takes the whole of the usufructs.

20. In the Act, 1950 changes were made in creating usufructory mortgage by inserting section 95. It is said, a raiyat cannot enter into any form of usufructory mortgage other than ''complete usufructory mortgage,'' the period of such mortgage shall be limited to seven years only for realization of the mortgagee''s dues from the usufruct of the land transferred by way of mortgage, the document must be registered, and after the completion of the period of seven years the land shall revert back to the mortgagor. Any contrary provision in any contract or deed in such a transaction shall be treated as void. In the proviso to sub-section (1), the mortgagor has been given the right to redeem the land mortgaged before the expiry of seven years on payment of the proportionate sum to the mortgagee. The period of ''seven'' years was substituted for the word ''fifteen'' by Ordinance XXI of 1969.

21. Section 95A was also inserted by PO 88 of 1972 which lays down that any transfer of a holding either by way of ''sale with an agreement to recovery'' and the transferee gets possession of thereof for a specified period in exchange of the consideration, such transaction be deemed to be a complete usufructory mortgage for a period not exceeding seven years. This provision shall supersede other provisions of law, that is to say, section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act and section 95 of Act, 1950 by reason of the use of the expression ''Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law''. This non-obstante clause will override all other pro-visions for entering into any form of usufructory mortgage and the provisions contained in section 95 shall apply to such transfer. In this section a transaction of ''an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey'' has also been recognized as mortgage by way of amendment. The position as it stands now is that though it is not a mortgage within the meaning of section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act, it is a mortgage within the meaning of section 95A. In view of such change by way of addition of a transaction of a sale with a condition to repurchase to be a complete usufructory mortgage, the question that requires to be considered is whether earlier views taken by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and the Supreme Court of India on construction of the proviso to section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act have any significance or in the alternative, have any persuasive value. After the amendment, in such transaction the relationship of debtor and creditor does subsist. It is now a partial transfer and such partial transfer does not confer all rights on the purchaser in the property.

22. In Abdus Salam Sheikh vs Rupsa Rani Shil, 49 DLR (AD) 71, BB Roy Chowdhury, J argued that the underlying object of inserting section 95A is to rescue a raiyat from the clutches of the money lenders who taking advantage of the poverty of the raiyat force him to enter into a disadvantageous deal by means of getting a registered kabala from the raiyat, themselves executing an unregistered agreement for reconveyance. Similar arguments were made by BH Chowdhury, J in Haji Abdul Gani (Supra) "the raiyat is to be rescued from the clutches of the money lenders or mohajans who taking advantage of the poverty of the raiyat would force him to enter into a disadvantageous deal. To protect a raiyat from such transactions, the law makers came to his rescue prohibiting him from entering into any kind of mortgage other than complete usufructuary mortgage and the maximum period for which he could transfer his land was reduced to seven years whereupon the debt including the principal and interest stands liquidated and on an application before the authorised officer the raiyat could be put back into possession".

23. Sections 95 and 95A are special laws promulgated for the protection of poor tenants, maliks or raiyats from the clutches of the moneyed men or ex-landlords for restoration of mortgaged property in a summary manner without the intervention of the court and payment of court fees. But these provisions, however, do not take away right of redemption of mortgaged property available to a mortgagor by filing a suit for redemption. It being a special privilege afforded to poor cultivators, the latter would choose the forum for their remedy. If they choose to abandon this special forum, section 95 does not prohibit or restrict them from availing the other forum available under the old law before providing this special forum. The question as regards past and closed transaction is to be seen in relation to the choice of forum. If the mortgagor chooses the special forum provided by sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 95 of Act, 1950, then the opinions expressed in Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat vs Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat, 16 BLD (AD) 210 =1 BLC (AD) 90 (para 11), and Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani, 32 DLR (AD) 233 (Para 11) will hold the field but this special remedy does not altogether oust the remedy provided in the civil Court.

24. In Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat (supra) it was observed that the transaction which attracts section 95A shall be deemed to be a complete usufructory mortgage and that to attract the application of section 95A the transaction must be a subsisting one on the date of promulgation of President''s Order No. PO 88 of 1972 (3-8-72) and the transactions which are not alive on that date are to be treated as transactions past and closed''. In Haji Abdul Gani (supra), it was observed that the transaction which attracts sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 95 are not understood in the light of the Transfer of Property Act because those are to be understood in the light of enactment in question. B.H. Chowdhury, J. further observed those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President''s Order No.88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey, made whether before after the promulgation of President''s order No.88 of 1972; and (5) as for the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President''s Order No.88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed''. By inserting these provisions, section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act has not been repealed.

25. In the case of Abu Bakkar (Supra), Abu Bakkar instituted the suit for redemption of the land transferred by him in favour of the defendant on 11th November, 1953. He claimed that the transaction was a kot mortgage and the entire consideration of the mortgage was satisfied by the usufruct of the land during the period of eleven years. The defendant Nazir Ahmed claimed that the transaction was an out and out sale with a condition of reconveyance on repayment of the consideration within the period of five years and as no repayment was made within the period of five years, the transaction became absolute and the suit was barred by limitation. The trial Court dismissed the suit but the appellate Court reversed the finding and found the deed to be a usufructory mortgage and decreed the suit. The High Court Division was of the view that the transaction was an out and out sale and that suit was barred by limitation on the doctrine of past and closed transaction. This Division reversed the judgment observing that the introduction of section 95A by PO 88 of 1972 does not touch the period of usufructuary mortgage nor does it affect the period of limitation for redemption of the holding by a suit if filed within a period of sixty years. It was observed that the amendment relates to two new provisions.

''one is that if, on the expiry of the period of a mortgage, the mortgagee does not restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, then the Sub-Divisional Magistrate shall on an application by the mortgagor, restore possession to the mortgagor by evicting the mortgagee. In other words, for getting back possession of a mortgaged land the mortgagor need not file any redemption suit, and he will get quick remedy by way of an application to the Sub-divisional Magistrate. The other provision in the amendment is that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law in force, any transfer of a land by an out and out sale with a condition for reconveyance shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding seven years on the expiry of which the mortgagor may get back possession by application to the sub-divisional Magistrate.''

26. In that case also this Division reaffirmed the views taken in Haji Abdul Gani Biswas (supra) while considering the true intent and purpose for inserting sections 95 and 95A in the Act of 1950 observing that if no possession is given by the mortgagor, he may file a suit for redemption within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of his right of redemption, and this amendment does not ''affect the period of limitation for redemption suit which is 60 years.'' In Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat [16 BLD (AD) 210 = 1 BLC (AD) 90), the views taken in Abu Bakkar (34 DLR (AD) 237] were also approved and observed that ''the views taken in Haji Abdul Gani Biswas (32 DLR (AD) 233) do not in any way seem to be in conflict with the decision cited i.e. 34 DLR (AD) 237''.

27. In Asmat Ali vs Abdul Rafique Mridha, 20 BLD (AD) 197 = 52 DLR (AD) 132: a suit was instituted for redemption of mortgage deed executed in 1962. It was stipulated in the deed that the mortgagor or his successors would be able to reconvey the property within 10 years from the date of mortgage. The mortgagor requested to deliver possession of the property of the land, to which, the mortgagees refused. The defendants claimed that the transaction was an out and out sale and that the suit was not maintainable. The trial Court as well as the appellate court found that the suit for redemption is maintainable and the same having been filed within 60 years from the accrual of the cause of action, the suit was maintainable. The High Court Division reversed the findings holding that the suit was barred by limitation. This Division by majority reversed the judgment and restored the decree passed by the trial Court and affirmed the opinion expressed in Haji Abdul Gani Biswas (supra) observing: ''PO 88 of 1972 created special forum for restoration of mortgaged property. But it did not take away right of redemption available to a mortgagor by filing a suit under Order 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure.''

28. In Rama Devi vs Dilip Singh. (2008) 7 SCC 105 referred by Mr Bhuiyan, Rama Devi executed a deed on 15th May, 1974 in respect of some land as she needed money for her business. It was recited that in case of an amount of 13,000 plus interest at the rate of 24% was returned by her within a period of 5 years, the land would be reconveyed to her. She requested the defendants to transfer the land but the latter refused the request and then she instituted the suit for redemption. The defendant admitted the execution of the deed but contended that it was an out and out sale. The Court below as well as High Court held that the deed was not a mortgage but it was in fact a sale and dismissed the suit. The Supreme Court while affirming the views taken by the High Court was of the opinion that a document has to be interpreted as a whole in order to arrive at a conclusion as to its true meaning and import and to determine whether it was a mortgage by way of conditional sale or a sale out right. Thereafter, on consideration of the oral and documentary evidence it was held that since possession was delivered at the time of execution of the deed, the vendor lost all her rights in the property by virtue of the deeming provisions of section 164 of UP Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 applicable to the case which was a special law. So the case is quite distinguishable and not applicable in this case.

29. The case of Ganu Mia vs Abdul labium 10 DLR 636 referred by Mr Bhuiyan was a case under Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940 and the application was made to the trial Court claiming the transaction as kot mortgage; the deed was executed sometime in 1944. The opposite party resisted the claim stating that the application was not maintainable, inasmuch as, the transaction was an out and out sale and not a mortgage by conditional sale. The trial Court allowed the application holding that the transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale. The appellate Court, however, held that the transaction was an out and out sale with a condition of repurchase and not a mortgage by conditional sale. A Single Bench of the High Court Division on construction of the documents noticed the beginning words ''kabala for absolute sale of immovable property free from encumbrance'' and came to the conclusion that the ''documents themselves seem that these are absolute sale of the land described therein.'' So this case is also quite distinguishable and not applicable in this case.

30. The conspectus of the above discussions is that in order to decide a transaction to be a mortgage by conditional sale or a sale with a condition of re-purchase, or the transaction is past and closed, the first and foremost thing to be looked into is whether the words used in the deed sufficiently indicate an intention of the parties to create a security for the debt; secondly, if the intention of the parties has been ambiguously expressed; the nomenclature of the deed is to be looked into which will be useful for determining the nature of the transaction; thirdly, whether the relationship of borrower and lender exists between the parties; and finally, the transaction was created by a single deed or by different deeds. The doctrine of past and closed transaction will be applicable in respect of a transaction which is not alive on the date of promulgation of PO 88 of 1972 and the same can be determined on the construction of the deed. The special forum created by section 95 of Act, 1950 does not affect the period of limitation for redemption of the land if the transaction between the parties is found to be one of a mortgage by conditional sale and if the suit is filed within a period of sixty years from the date of accrual of right.

31. Taking these preconditions in mind, let us consider the deed in question. In the prefix of the deed the words ''৫ সনা ম্যাদী কবলা সংখ্যা ১০০০’ have been mentioned and in the recitals, the following words have been stated: “জমিন জমা ৫ পাঁচ সেনা ম্যাদী কবলা পত্র মিদং আগে চকরিয়া থানায় আন্তঃপাত্তি পেকুয়া মৌজায় স্থিত নিম্ন তপশিলাদির লিখিত মহল মালিকানের অধিনীয় মোট জমি জমার আন্দর জমিন জমা আপনার নিকট ম্যাদী বিক্রয় করিয়া তাহার প্রকৃত মূল্য মং ১,০০০ এক হাজার টাকা অদ্য নগদ আপনার কার্যকারক মুন্সি ছিদ্দিক আহমদের মারফতে গ্রহন করিলাম ৷ ইহাতে আপনি আমার স্বত্বে সত্যবান ইেয়৷ আমার আসল দখলমতে আসল দখল করতঃ সন সন উপরিন্থের কর আদায় দিয়া বক্রী মুনাফা পরম মুখে ভোপবান থাকেন তৎপতি আমার কি আমার ওয়ারিশানের দাবী দাওয়া নাই ও রহিল না । প্রকাশে আপনার ম্যাদি কবলা মুক্ত তােগদখলের হানী হয় । ইহা প্রকাশ থাকে যে ম্যাদ মধ্যে যে কোন সনের চৈত্র মাসে আপনার আসল টাকা আদায় করিয়া দিলে অত্র দলিল ও খাজনা আদায়ের দাখিলা সহ জমিন আমাদের দখলে ছাড়িয়া দিবেন। ম্যাদ মধ্যে আপনার আসল টাকা আদায় করিতে না পারিলে ম্যাদ অবসানে আদালত ক্রমে বরবাদ সিদ্দ পূর্বক নিদ্দায় কবলা গন্য করতে সম হইবেন।”

32. We noticed from the deed as quoted above, instead of using the word বিক্রয় (sale), the wordy ম্যাদী (period) was used. Though in the recitals the word বিক্রয় (sale) was also used, it was qualified by the word ম্যাদী (period). The use of the word ''sale'' is conditional and intended as security for the debt, inasmuch as in place of sale deed it was mentioned as conditional sale. It was also recited that if the recipient of the deed failed to hand over possession on the demand of the vendors on repayment of principal amount within the month of Chaitra in any year, they would be entitled to redeem the land through the process of the court after the expiry of the period of 5 years. The parties intended to execute the deed for a limited period of 5 years in respect of the land which could be redeemed within the said period if the vendors had paid the amount received from the vendee. If the intention of the parties is to create a security for a debt, it will be a mortgage.

<u>33. So it is apparent that the land was given for the security of the debt and on payment of the debt, the vendee was bound to give back the land. The parties intended to create a relationship of borrower and lender which is apparent on a plain reading of the deed. There is no ambiguity in the language employed in the deed and the intention of the parties can be inferred from the contents of the deed. The relationship of debtor and creditor does not cease to exist in the case and it is not an absolute sale merely because the vendors stipulated that they shall have a right to repurchase. There is, therefore, no doubt that the transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale within the meaning of section 58(c) of the Transfer of property Act and the period of limitation for redemption of such mortgage is 60 years from the date of expiry of years from 21 April 1941. The suit is, therefore, not barred by limitation or in the alternative, the transaction is not past and closed one.</u>

34. The learned Munsif held that the suit as framed is maintainable; that the transaction in question was a mortgage and that the period of limitation is 60 years for redemption of mortgage. The court of appeal below, on the other hand, held that the transaction being out and out sale, the question of redemption of mortgage did not exist; that plaintiffs remedy lay not by way of the suit as framed but by way of appeal against the decision of Debt Settlement Board; and that the suit is barred by limitation. The High Court Division on construction of the impugned deed held that the transaction was a mortgage within the meaning of section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 95 of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act, and not sale with a condition of repurchase.

35. The High Court Division unnecessarily took pains by taking into consideration of section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act and sections 95 and 95A of the Act of 1950 and arrived at the conclusion that the transaction was a complete usufructuary mortgage in view of section 95A of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act incorporated by PO 88 of 1972. It failed to notice that the respondents did not choose the special forum created by the statute. The respondents treated the transaction as one of mortgage by conditional sale and instituted the suit for redemption of mortgage. They did not opt to redeem the mortgage under section 95. The High Court Division was of the view that in view of the words used in second part of section 95A, "or whether transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of such holding or portion or share thereof for a specified period in lieu of such consideration, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage the relief claimed in the suit would be regulated by section 95A even if the plaintiffs instituted the suit for redemption of mortgage", the law will equally be applicable for redemption of mortgages created at any time.

36. There is no recital in the deed that the transferee would enjoy the usufructs of the land for specified period in lieu of the money received by her. It was clearly recited in the deed that the vendors would be entitled to recover the land within a period of five years on repayment of the amount of loan, and in case of failure to repay the said amount, they would be entitled to recover the land through the process of the Court. As observed above, the deed discloses a relationship between the parties as debtor and creditor. The debt subsists and a right to redeem remains with the debtors. The High Court Division failed to consider that after coming into force of Part-V of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act, the Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed. Though Part-V came into force first in Patuakhali on 5th August, 1954 and lastly in Faridpur on 5th August, 1965 by gazette Notifications, laws appended in the schedule to section 80 in their entirety repealed in those areas to the extent mentioned in the fourth column including the Bengal Tenancy Act, so much as those have not been repealed, as for example, the provisions of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act regarding the right of pre-emption as provided in that section shall apply in its entirety in those areas and not the provisions of section 96 of the Act in respect of cases where application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act were filed in courts and during the pendency of those applications, Part-V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force in those areas. Thus the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act repealed those previous Tenancy Laws save and except the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 and the Transfer of Property Act, and those unrepealed land laws along with Part V of the Act of 1950 have become the guiding laws of the country. Therefore, those findings are superfious but the ultimate decision of the High Court Division is correct.

Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J: This appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and decree dated the 12th day of July, 2000 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Appellate Decree (Second Appeal) No. 1086 of 1968 allowing the same.

38. Facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows:

The predecessors-in-interest of respondent Nos.1(a)-1(h), 2(a)-2(f), 3(a)-3(J), 4(a)-4(g), 5, 6(a)-6(e), 7(a)-(e), 8, 9(a)-9(e), 10-15, 16(a)-16(d), 17 and 18(a)-18(c) as plaintiffs filed Other Suit No. 107 of 1959 in the Court of Munsif, Cox''s Bazar impleading the appellant herein and others as defendants for recovery of khas possession of the lands fully described in the schedule to the plaint under 7(seven) heads, total area being 8.46 acres on redemption of the mortgage made on 22-4-1936.

39. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that the lands described in the schedule to the plaint (hereinafter referred to as the scheduled lands) belonged to plaintiff Nos. 1, 2, 9 and 10 and the predecessor-in-interest of plaintiff Nos. 3-8 in occupancy right. They mortgaged the scheduled lands to Omra Khatun on 22-4-1936 for a term of 5(five) years and put the mortgagee in possession of the mortgaged land. Omra Khatun died leaving behind defendant No. 1 as son and one daughter-Asia Khatun and father Maqbul Ahmed Chowdhury. On the death of Asia Khatun, her husband, defendant No. 2 and son, defendant No. 3, got her interest. On the death of Maqbul Ahmed Chowdhury, his interest devolved upon defendant Nos. 4-19. The defendants are in possession of the mortgaged lands. The mortgaged lands are of superior quality and produce good crops and by the usufructs of the lands, the mortgagee''s dues had been satisfied and therefore, the plaintiffs were entitled to get back the lands. As the defendants did not amicably restore back possession of the mortgaged lands to the plaintiffs, they were obliged to file the suit for the reliefs aforementioned.

40. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter-alia, that the suit was not maintainable in the present form and was barred by limitation. The disputed document in favour of Omra Khatun was not a mortgage deed, but an out and out sale deed. One part of the disputed lands was previously mortgaged with Badu Bibi and she was put into possession thereof and after the execution and registration of the deed dated 22-4-1936 (the disputed deed) in favour Omra Khatun, the plaintiffs could not put her into the possession of the lands at serial Nos. 2 and 3 of the schedule as the same were under the possession of the previous mortgagee, Badu Bibi. Subsequently, rents of the lands of serial Nos. 2 and 3 of the schedule fell into arrears for which those were sold in auction in execution of a decree and were auction purchased by Maqbul Ahmed Chowdhury, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 5-15(Maqbul Ahmed Chowdhury is the father of mortgagee, Omra Khatun). The land of serial No. 1 of the schedule was put to auction (sale) for arrears of rent in Certificate Case No. 934/1936-37 and was auction purchased by Abdul Jabbar, father of defendant No. 1. The land of serial No. 5 of the schedule was auction purchased by Emdadul Haque, defendant No.4. After auction purchase of the lands of serial Nos. 2 and 3 of the schedule by Maqbul Ahmed and serial No. 1 by defendant No. 1''s father, the respective auction purchaser took possession of those lands and subsequently, by an exchange Maqbul Ahmed gave the lands of serial Nos. 2 and 3 of the schedule to the father of defendant No. 1 in exchange for the property of serial No. 1 of the schedule and the heirs of Maqbul Ahmed are in possession of the lands of serial No.1 of the schedule by erecting homestead therein and defendant No.1 is in possession of the lands of serial Nos.2 and 3 of the schedule by making improvement at a huge cost. The plaintiffs were all along aware of these acts of possession of the disputed lands by the defendants by virtue of auction purchase, and exchange and, as such, they were estopped from raising the question of redemption of the mortgage on false pleas. The claim of the plaintiffs for redemption of the mortgage was dismissed by the Debt Settlement Board in a case brought by them. There being no existence of any mortgage as alleged by the plaintiffs, they were not entitled to get any relief as prayed for and the suit was liable to be dismissed.

41. Defendant No. 4 also filed a sec4rate written statement contending similar facts and taking similar stand as contended and taken by defendant No.1 in his written statement.

42. The trial Court decreed the suit by its judgment and decree dated the 24th day of March, 1964. 43. The appellant herein who was defendant No. 1 took an appeal being Other Appeal No. 168 of 1964 before the District Judge, Chittagong. The learned Subordinate Judge, who heard the appeal by his judgment and decree dated the 27th day of November, 1965, allowed it and dismissed the suit.

44. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, the plaintiffs filed Appeal from Appellate Decree (Second Appeal) No. 1086 of 1968 before the then High Court of Judicature at Dhaka now the High Court Division. A learned Judge of the Single Bench by the impugned judgment and decree allowed the same, set-aside the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court and restored those of the trial Court. Against the judgment and decree of the High Court Division, defendant No.1 filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1041 of 2000 before this Division and leave was granted to consider the submissions made on behalf of the appellant as follows:

"It is now submitted before us that in the instant case the parties agreed by the transaction in question that the period of mortgage will be for 5 years beginning from 22-4-1936. So the transaction cannot be said to be alive and subsisting on the date of promulgation of President''s Order No.88 of 1972 i.e. on 3-8-1992. It was past and closed transaction as such the plaintiff cannot claim redemption as the complete usufactory (sic) as contemplated under section 95-A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It has further been submitted that the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division having been made contrary to the decision reported in 1 BLC (AD) 90, 164, 49 DLR (AD) 228 is not sustainable in law inasmuch the impugned judgment is based on misreading of the decisions reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233, 34 DLR (AD) 237 and accordingly is not sustainable in law."

45. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant has submitted that the merit of the appeal would depend upon the construction of the deed dated 22-4-1936. According to Mr Bhuiyan if the deed is read as a whole, it would appear that it is an out and out sale deed and not a mortgage, therefore, the plaintiffs'' suit for recovery of khas possession on redemption of mortgage was not maintainable in law, but the trial Court as well as the High Court Division on misreading and misconstruction of the deed erroneously held that the deed in question (dated 22-4-1936) was a deed of mortgage and not an out and out sale deed. Mr Bhuiyan elaborating his submission has further submitted that from the deed dated 22-4-1936 it being clear that the relationship between the plaintiffs, the mortgagors and the mortgagee, Omra Khatun was not a debtor or creditor and the lands in question were not given as a security of any loan obtained by the plaintiffs, by no argument the deed in question can be treated as a deed of mortgage. He has lastly submitted that even if it were accepted that the deed in question is a deed of mortgage and not an out and out sale deed, in that case also the period of 5(five) years having already expired long before 3-8-1972, section 95A will have no application to the transaction which was past and closed and, as such, the High Court Division fell into an error in maintaining the decree passed by the trial Court. Mr Bhuiyan also reiterated his submission on the other point on which leave had been granted.

46. In support of his contentions Mr Bhuiyan has relied upon the cases of Manjabai Krishna Patil (dead) by LRS vs Raghunath Revaji Patil (2007) 12 SCC, 427, Rama Devi vs Dilip Singh (2008) 7 SCC, 105, Bhagwan Shahi vs Bhagwan Din, 17 Indian Appeals, 98, Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat vs Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat, 1 BLC (AD) (1996) 90 and 164, Niaz Ganu Mia vs Abdul Jabbar, 10 DLR (Dhaka) 636.

47. Mr Mustafa Niaz Mohammad, learned Counsel, appearing for the plaintiff-respondents, on the other hand, has submitted that in the deed itself, there being clear recital to the effect ‘৫ পাঁচ সনা ম্যাদী কবলা’ there is no scope to interpret the same as an out and out sale deed, and as the mortgagee and after her death, her heirs, failed to give back possession of the same to the plaintiffs on their request, their suit for khas possession on redemption of mortgage was quite maintainable in law, the trial Court and the High Court Division rightly decreed the same and therefore, no interference is called for with the impugned judgment and decree and the appeal be dismissed. He relied upon the cases of Abu Bakkar vs Nazir Ahmed, 34 DLR (AD) 237 and Md Nasirullah vs Md Ziauddin Khan, 12 MLR (AD) 329.

48. Before considering the propriety of the submissions of the learned Counsel of the respective parties, let us see the findings of the Courts below.

49. From the judgment of the trial Court, it appears that, on consideration of the recitals of the deed in question it came to the clear finding that it was a pure and simple deed of mortgage and not an out and out sale deed as claimed by the defendants and therefore, the plaintiffs were entitled to redeem it and the suit was not barred by limitation as "it is governed by 60 years." The first Appellate Court held that the deed in question was an out and out sale deed with a condition of repurchase at the option of the transferor to be exercised within five years ignoring the clause about foreclosure in the deed itself on the observation that:

"In this context the additional clause about foreclosure in this document to my mind does not keep in with the intentions of the parties as expressed by the language used in the document, Exhibit A and Ddbit 1 his (sic) it would be this) condition of fore-closure to my mind is nothing but a redundant clause having in view the clear intentions expressed by the language used in the clause."

50. The High Court Division on consideration of the terms ''mortgage'', ''complete usufructuary mortgage'' and the provisions of President''s Order Nos. 88 of 1972, 136 of 1972, 24 of 1973, and relying upon the decisions in the cases of Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani, 32 DLR (AD) 233, Abu Bakkar vs Nazir Ahmed, 34 DLR (AD) 237 and Jahir Ahmed vs Badsha Mia Sowadagar, 36 DLR 90 held that: "So from all angles of views the transaction in question cannot be termed other than complete usufructuary mortgage subject to redemption within 60 years."

51. The deed in question was exhibited by both parties, the plaintiffs produced its certified copy, defendant No.1 produced its original and were marked as exhibit-''1'' and ''Ka'' respectively. The preamble of the deed is ‘৫ পাঁচ সনা ম্যাদী কবলা’ and in the body of the deed also it has been written as ‘৫ পাঁচ সনা ম্যাদী কবলা’. In the body of the deed as also found by Appellate Court there is a clear clause for foreclosure. And it is an admitted fact that the possession of the lands transferred by the deed in question was handed over to the mortgagee and after her death her heirs, namely, the defendants are in possession thereof and thus, they have enjoyed the usufructs of the mortgaged land; when in the deed itself there is a clause for foreclosure the first Appellate Court could not avoid that on the plea that the same was a redundant one and on the further plea that clause about foreclosure "does not keep in with the intentions of the parties". So, we find no difficulty in concurring with the trial Court as affirmed by the High Court Division that the deed in question (Ext-T and Ext-''Ka'') is a deed of mortgage and not an out and out sale deed. Therefore, we find no substance in the submission of Mr Bhuiyan that the deed in question is not a deed of mortgage, but an out and out sale deed.''

52. Since the deed in question is a deed of mortgage, and there cannot be any other mortgage than usufructuary mortgage after 1928 when section 26G was inserted in the Bengal Tenancy Act by Act IV of 1928, it is subject to redemption at the option of the mortgagor within 60 years as provided in article 148 of the Limitation Act, the plaintiffs rightly brought the suit for redemption of the mortgage created by the deed.

53. The facts of the instant case are exactly the same as in the case of Abu Bakkar vs Nazir Ahmed, 34 DLR (AD) 237. In that case leave was granted to consider whether the suit was barred by limitation as well as by the doctrine of past and closed transaction and this Division considering the finding of the trial Court held that "though there is a condition for re-conveyance within a period of 5 years, yet it is in fact usufructuary mortgage which has been referred to in the instrument as “মেয়াদী নির্দায় কবালা” all the dues under the mortgage deed were extinguished by the produce of the land allowed the appeal on the view that

"5. . . . The maximum period for which a usufructuary mortgage can be entered into was fifteen years under section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. But by Ordinance No. XXI of 1969, section 95 was amended and thereby the maximum period for a usufructuary mortgage was reduced to seven years. And unless earlier redeemed by repayment of the consideration a mortgagor acquires right to redemption on the expiry of the maximum period of seven years, and if the mortgage (sic) does not voluntarily restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, the latter may file a suit for redemption within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of his right of redemption. In this case, the suit was filed just on the accrual of the right of redemption and, as such, it is not barred by limitation.

6. Section 95 has been again amended by the President''s Order No.88 of 1972 with effect from 3 August, 1972, but this amendment did not touch the period of a usufructuary mortgage which is still 7 years, nor did is affect the period of limitation for redemption suit which is 60 years. The amendment relates to two new provisions. One is that if, on the expiry of the period of a mortgage, the mortgagee does not restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, then the Sub-Divisional Magistrate shall, on an application by the mortgagor, restore possession to the mortgagor by evicting the mortgagee. In other words, for getting back possession of a mortgaged land the mortgagor need not file any redemption suit, but may get quick remedy by an application to the Sub-Division Magistrate. The other provisions in the amendment is that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law in force, any transfer of a land by an out and out sale with a condition for reconveyance shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 years on the expiry of which the mortgagor may get back possession by an application to the Sub-Divisional Magistrate. The High Court Division in view of its own conclusion that the transaction under Ext.A is an out and out sale, considered whether this sale should be deemed to be a usufructuary mortgage and found that the transaction was past and closed. But since the transaction is, as we have found, a mortgage no question arises whether it should be treated as mortgage."

54. The right of a mortgagor to redeem the mortgaged land by way of filing a mortgage suit within 60 years from the date of accrual of such right of redemption without taking recourse to the quick remedy as provided in section 95 of the Act, 1950 also came up for Consideration before this Division in the case of Md Nasirullah vs Md Ziauddin Khan reported in 12 MLR (AD) 329 and in that case while maintaining the decision of the High Court Division this Division held:

"7. The High Court Division relying on the above decision [34 DLR (AD) 237] held that the right of redemption shall accrue after 12 years from 1936, date of mortgage deed and the suit has been filed within a period of 60 years. Accordingly both the courts below committed a gross error of law in construing the President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 and in holding that the mortgage deed was executed in 1936 and section 95 of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act was amended by promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 with effect from 3-8-1972 and the transaction is a past and closed one, overlooking the vital fact that the mortgagor''s right of redemption within a period of 60 years limitation has not been taken away by president''s Order No. 88 of 1972 rather by promulgating President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 a quick remedy has been made available to a raiyat but it did not in any way affect the long practiced remedy of the right of redemption of mortgage by filing a suit within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of the right of redemption."

55. Like the above mentioned two reported cases, in the instant case, the mortgage deed was executed on 22-4-1936, the suit was filed on 22-6-1959, that is, well within the period of 60 years from the date of expiry of the mortgage period of 5 (five) years (as per the terms of the deed). One of the grievances of the appellant as apparent from the leave granting order is that the High Court Division passed the impugned judgment and decree contrary to the principle of law enunciated by this Division in the cases of Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat vs Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat, 1 BLC (AD) 90 and Anwaruddin Bepari vs Assistant Commissioner (Land) reported in the same volume page 164 (there is no case in 49 DLR (AD) 228 on the point of law involved in this appeal as noted in the leave granting order). Let us see whether this grievance is correct.

56. The first case of 1 BLC arose out of a judgment and order passed in a writ petition declaring the order of Additional Commissioner, Khulna Division dated 24-3-1988 in Redemption Appeal No.213 of 1985 "as of no legal effect." Facts of that case were that respondent No. 1 purchased one acre of land from the appellant by a registered kabala dated 24-6-1967 for a consideration of Taka 2,000. On the same date he executed a registered agreement to reconvey the kabala if the consideration money was repaid within 4 years from that date. A proceeding started by the appellant under the Act, 1950 for redemption of the kabala land vide Miscellaneous Case No.922BK /73-74 was dismissed by the Circle Officer (Revenue), Bakergonj by his order dated 3-2-1983 and appeal from the said order was also dismissed the Additional Deputy Commissioner Revenue) on 1-7-1985, upon a further appeal the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Khulna by his order dated 24-3-1988 allowed the appeal and ordered redemption of the land as prayed for by the appellant in his miscellaneous case which was set-aside by the High Court Division in the writ petition. Further facts were that the appellant also filed Miscellaneous Case No.1227 of 1972-73 before the then Sub-divisional Officer, Barisal (South) to get the land redeemed. During the pendency of the needing the appellant filed Title Suit No. 287 of 1979 in the Second Court of Munsif, Barisal for specific performance of contract on the basis of the aforesaid agreement for reconveyance which was dismissed on 17-4-1980 on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation. The appellant took an appeal, Title Appeal No. 120 1980, which was also dismissed by the District Judge, Bakergonj on 26-6-1981. In this context this Division dismissed the appeal on the view that the parties agreed to the transaction in question that the period of mortgage will be for 4 years beginning from 24-6-1967. So, the transaction cannot be alive and subsisting on the date of promulgation, of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972, i.e., 3-8-1972. It was a transaction past and closed. In this case, the view taken in 34 DLR (AD) 237 as quoted above was endorsed. The striking feature of the instant case and the case reported in 1 BLC (AD) 90 is that in the instant case a regular suit for redemption of the mortgaged land was filed, but in the reported case recourse was taken to the provisions of section 95 of the Act, 1950 after the promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 on 3-8-1972. The facts of the second case of 1 BLC are almost similar to the first case. And we consider it sufficient to say that in this case also no suit for redemption was filed and recourse was taken under the provisions of section 95 of the Act, 1950 after the expiry of the right of reconveyance of respondent No. 4 as per terms of the contemporaneous agreement which expired on 10-1-1972 and this Division allowed the appeal declaring the order passed by respondent No.1, Assistant Commissioner (Land), Lauhajang on 10-5-1992 directing the appellant to hand over possession of the disputed land to respondent No.4 to have been passed without lawful authority and be of no legal effect on the same view taken in the first case. Facts of the instant case being quite dis-similar from the two BLC cases; the principle of law enunciated therein has got no manner of application in the instant case.

57. So far as the case reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233 is concerned, it appears that 46 appeals arising out of the judgment and order passed in 46 writ petitions were heard analogously; in none of those cases, any suit for redemption was filed. From the judgment, it appears that fact of one case (writ petition No. 85 of 74) only was stated which are that respondent No.1 purchased the land from respondent No. 2 with an agreement to reconvey the same. The agreement was dated 26-4-63 which stipulated that the land would be reconveyed if the money was repaid within 10 years. Respondent No. 3 made an application under sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 95 of the Act, 1950 to respondent No. 2 for restoration of possession of the said land. The petition was allowed on 30-3-73 and thereafter respondent No. 1 filed the writ petition urging, inter-alia, that the said order was without lawful authority, inasmuch as section 95A of the aforesaid Act did not cover the case of the pure sale with an agreement to reconvey. An out and out sale accompanied by an agreement for reconveyance was within the purview of the President''s Nos. 88 and 136 of 1972 and No.24 of 1973 whereby provisions of section 95 of the Act, 1950 have been amended and a new section being section 95A has been inserted in the Act, 1950. The High Court Division disposed of the said writ petition along with other writ petitions by one judgment as the same question of law of public importance had been raised and on consideration of which a certificate was also granted. In the writ petitions vires of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 whereby section 95A was inserted and the constitutionality of President''s Order No.24 of 1973.were challenged. The High Court Division made all the Rules absolute with the findings, inter-alia, that (a) a transaction of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey within the meaning of section 95A must be in sense a mortgage; (b) a transaction of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey is not a transaction within the ambit of section 95A; (c) section 95A has no application to a transaction which has been passed and closed before the relevant President''s Order was promulgated; (d) section 95A cannot be invoked in respect of a transaction which has been entered into before Part-V of the Act, 1950 came into operation in the area in which the land in question lies. In that case this Division held that:

"Our conclusions, therefore, are that the President''s Order Nos. 88 and 136 of 1972 and No. 24 of 1973 are all valid legislation for effecting necessary amendments in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and those laws cannot be attacked on the ground of ultra vires. (2) any transfer of a holding or part thereof by a raiyat either by way of out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period of maximum 7 years and the provisions of section 95(4) and (5) shall apply to such transfers; (3) and such transfers are not to be understood in the light of the Transfer of Property Act because those are to be understood in the light of the enactment in question: (4) those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey, made whether before or after the promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972: and (5) as for the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed."

<u>58. From a reading of this case, it. does not appear that the question as to the right of redemption of a mortgage by way of filing a suit in civil court within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of such right was raised and decided, but this question was precisely raised and decided in 34 DLR (AD) 237 and 12 MLR (AD) 329. And we see no reason to take a view different from the views taken therein by this Division.</u>

<u>59. From the impugned judgment, it appears that the High Court Division took notice of the conclusions arrived at by this Division in the case of Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani Biswas (supra) on the question of applicability of section 95 and 95A of the Act, 1950 correctly in deciding the point at issue in the instant case. Therefore, we find no merit in the submission that the High Court Division passed the impugned judgment and decree "contrary to the decision reported in 1 BLC (AD) 90, 164" and also "on misreading of the decisions reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233, 34 DLR (AD) 237."</u>

60. Since we have found that the deed in question (22-4-1936) is a deed of mortgage and not an out and out sale deed and the suit for redemption maintainable, the other ancillary point argued by Mr Bhuiyan and the citations referred to by him in that respect do not deserve any consideration.

61. In conclusion, we do not find any merits in the appeal. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed. There will be no order as to costs.

Nazmun Ara Sultana J: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my brothers, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J and Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the reasoning and findings given by Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J.

Syed Mahmud Hossain J : I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my brothers, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J and Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the reasoning and findings given by Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J.

Muhammad Imman Ali J: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my brothers, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J. and Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I appreciate the reasoning’s given by my learned brothers and agree that the appeal is liable to be dismissed.

Md Shamsul Huda J: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my brothers, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J and Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J I agree with the reasoning and findings given by my learned brother, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J.

End.

caseno: Writ Petition No. 3285 of 2009 & No.2829 of 2006.
lawyer:
Ekramul Islam and Sheikh ReajulHaque Advocates—For the Petitioners.
Munsurul Haq Chowdhury, Senior Advocate with Quamrul Hoque Siddiquee, SM Rezaul Karim, Md Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan, Advocates—For the Respondent. 
Raja Debashish Roy Chowdhury, Advocate with Sara Hussain, Advocate (the Intervenor)—For the Respondent.
parties:
Abrechai Mog and others ------ Petitioner
Vs
District Judge, Khagrachari and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Farah Mahbub J: Since common question of law and facts are involved in both the Rules Nisi as such, those have been heard together and are being disposed of by this single judgment.

2. In writ petition No. 3285 of 2009 a Rule Nisi has been issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh, calling upon the respondents concerned to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 22-9-1996 (Annexure-A) passed by the respondent No. 2, the Deputy Commissioner, Khagrachari and the ex-officio Civil Judge in connection with Civil Suit No. 20 of 1992 which has been upheld upto the Land Appeal Board, Dhaka directing vide order dated 12-3-2006 to make partition of 24.30 acres of land and opening a separate khatian in Volume 6, page 81 by the respondent No. 5 in favour of respondent Nos. 9-13 pursuant to Namjari Case No. 165 of 1997 (Annexure-B) should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

3. In writ petition No. 2829 of 2006 the impugned judgment and order dated 12-3-2001 passed by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong Division, Chittagong, respondent No. 4 in Civil Appeal (Khagrachari) Case No. 84 of 1997 (Annexure-C) disallowing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 22-9-1996, passed by the Deputy Commissioner, and ex-officio Civil Judge, Khagrachari, in Civil Suit No. 20 of 1992 allowing the suit for partition, is under challenge. 4. Common facts, in brief, are that late Dogyo Mog (a member of Marma community) was the original owner of the land in question measuring 24.30 acres of land who died in the year 1974 leaving behind two daughters, named Aowa Mogini and Abetu Mogini who shad inherited the said property being the successive heirs bearing Dag Nos. 689(full), 887 (full), 1037 (part), 1038 (part), 1040 (part), 1041 (part), 1065 (full), 1072 (full), 1073 (full), 1075 (full), 1076 (full), 1077 (full), 1078 (full), 1079 (part), 1112 (part), 1118 (part), 1143 (full), 1144 (full), 1040/1236 (part), look to 2676/3361 (full), 2675 (full), 1242 (full), 1180 (part), 1276 (full) appertaining to khatian No. 159 under 262 Golabari Mouza, Police Station-Khagrachari Sadar, District-Khagrachari Hill District (Annexure-B).

5. It has been stated that Aowa Mogini, one of the daughters of late Dogyo Mog, was insane as well as unmarried; thus, Abetu Mogini, her other sister became the sole successor of the entire property i.e., 24.30 acres of land. However, Abetu Mogini had 3(three) daughters named, Kraynori Mogini, Pusuma Mogini and Aungkra Mogini.

6. It has also been stated that during the lifetime of Dugyo Mog, Abetu Mogini, one of his daughters, had divided the said property along with possession amongst her 3(three) daughters giving Kraynory Mogini 8.10 acres(113), Pusuma Mogini 10.00 acres, for she was looking after the welfare of Aowa Mogini and gave the rest about 6.20 acres to Aunkra Mogini. It was, however, verbally settled amongst them that after the death of Aowa Mogini, the excess land (about 2.00 acres) would be vested back to Aungkra Mogini from Pusuma Mogini, so that each would get 1/3 share equally (8.30 acres out of 24.30) according to the "social custom" of the Marma community.

7. It has further been stated that Dugyo Mog expired in the year 1974 while he was in the house of Kraynori Mogini, one of his grand daughters who earlier died in 1972 with the aforesaid 8-10 acres of land as inherited from her mother Abetu Mogini. However, Kraynori Mogini had 3(three) daughters named Krajai Mogini, Aproaprue (Apaprue) Mogini (Writ Petitioner No. 8) of writ petition No. 3285 of 2009, Krasong Mogini and one son Chailapru Marma (respondent No.6).

8. It has also been stated that petitioner No.1 of writ petition No. 3285 of 2009 Abrechai Marma married 2(two) daughters of Kraynori Mogini, firstly he got married to Krajai Mogini and after her death, Krasong Mogini who also died at a later period. Consequent thereto Dugyo Mog while he was alive was the only de-facto guardian of all the sons and daughters of Kraynori Mogini including respondent No. 6, Chailapru Marma, for they were minors in the year 1972 to 1974.

9. However, Aungkra Mogini died leaving behind two sons named, Niyong Chowdhury and Sathong Chowdhury (respondent Nos. 7 and 8). It has been contended that Pusuma Mogini died in 1982 with 10 acres of land before the death of her insane aunt Aowa Mogini, who died in 1996. As such, question of giving back 2.00 acres of land during her life time to her sister Aunkra Mogini and her successors could not arise.

10. However, Pusuma Mogini died leaving behind 5(five) sons named Mongsajai Mog, Suijai Mog, Aungpru Mog, Hola Hathoi Mog and Apaise Mog, respondent Nos. 9-13.

11. In this regard it has been stated that out of 6.00 acres of land, as devolved upon Aungkra Mogini, the respondent government had meanwhile acquired 2 (two) acres of land in connection with the land acquisition case.

12. It has been contended emphatically that it was known to all that after the expiry of Aowa Mogini 2(two) acres of land, which was earlier given to Pasuma Mogini to look after her aunt Aowa Mogini being insane, would go to the respective successors of Aungkra Mogini named, Niyong Chowdhury and Sathaung Chowdhury, from the respective successors of Pusuma Mogini.

13. The cause of action arose when in violation of the Marma social custom and with malafide intention not to give back that 2.00 acres of land to the successors of Aungkra Mogini some of the successors of Pusuma Mogini (respondent Nos. 9-13) had managed to procure a succession certificate in the name of Aowa Mogini showing her as one of the successors of late Dugyo Mog.

14. Under the situation 2(two) sons of Aungkra Mogini named Niyong Chowdhury and Sathaung Chowdhury (respondent Nos. 6 and 7) as plaintiffs instituted Civil Suit No. 20 of 1992 on 9-6-1992, before the Court of Deputy Commissioner and the ex-officio Civil Judge, Khagrachari, respondent No. 2, for separate khatian as per possession and title of the inherited land of late Dogyo Mog impleading the respective successors of late Pusuma Mogini as defendant Nos. (Ka) 1-7 and also the successors of late Kraynori Mogini as defendant Nos. (Kha) 8-11 (Annexure-C). The defendants, how-ever, duly entered appearance in the said civil suit by filing written statement controverting the statements so made therein (Annexure-C-2).

15. However, prior to that on 2-6-2002 (Annexure-C-1) the concerned Mouza Headman sent an office letter to the Deputy Com-missioner, Chittagong, respondent No. 2 for a detail report regarding the property of late Dogyo Mog. He also made a prayer for staying operation of the succession certificate so obtained in connection with Miscellaneous Case Nos. 110, 65, and 98 all of 1990 with a view to settle the issue amicably.

16. Conversely, Chailaprue Marma, son of Kraynori Mogini, the defendant No.8 of Civil Suit No. 20 of 1992, as plaintiff instituted another Civil Suit bearing No. 20 of 1990 impleading Abrechai Mog, Apaprue Mogini, (petitioner-8), Krasong Mogini both daughters of Baikyo Mog, and Niyong Chowdhury, Sathong Chowdhury, both sons of Aungkra Mogini as defendant Nos. 1-6 respectively contending, inter-alia, that he was entitled to entirely get 1/3 share (8.30 acres of land) of late Kraynori Mogini being her only son, but the defendant No. 1 (petitioner No.1 of writ petition No. 3285 of 2009 ) being the brother-in-law of his two sisters Krajai Mogini and after her death Krasong Mogini was enjoying possession of 4.00 acres of land. However, the defendants duly submitted written statement denying the assertions so made by the said plaintiff.

17. Initially, trial of both the suits was held , before the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong on behalf of the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong who subsequently conduct-ed an inquiry in the presence of the respective contending parties through the Thana Nirbahi Officer, Khagrachari. In the enquiry report he duly opined for division of the property in question in 3(three) parts and to give share to each of the 3(three) daughters of late Dogyo Mog. The said report was duly sent to the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong for necessary approval on 22-2-1993 (Annexure-D). 18. Ultimately, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Khagrachari considering the plaint, written statement, report of the Headman, the inquiry report of the Thana Nirbahi Officer, Khagrachari Sadar and after hearing both the parties recommended, inter alia,
