parties:
Tae Hung Packaging (BD) Limited and others------  Appellants
vs
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 8th day of March, 2010, 17th day of December, 2010 & 20th day of May, 2010 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.7610 of 2008, 10164 of 2007 and 10171 of 2007).
full_judgment:
Md Muzammel Hossain CJ: I have gone through the judgments delivered by my learned brother, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J and my learned brother, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J I agree with the judgment of my learned brother, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J.

SK Sinha J : I have read the draft copy of the judgment prepared by my learned brethren Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J while agreeing with my learned brethren that these appeals should be dismissed, I would like to express my opinion separately on the question of the High Court Division's power to quash a criminal proceeding in exercise of powers under Article 102 of the Constitution. We have come across in a number of cases and find the High Court Division is not maintaining uniformity in entertaining and disposing of petitions for quashing criminal proceedings. Some Benches have entertained and disposed of writ petitions for quashing a proceeding in exercise of powers under Article 102 of the Constitution while other Benches have entertained petitions under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure on the same subject matter. Some Benches are of the opinion that a criminal proceeding can be quashed at the initial stage of investigation and some other Benches have taken different views. As a result, accumulation of number of cases in the docket is on the rise. Over and above, due to this reason of filing cases in different jurisdictions, we find no uniformity in the judgments on the point of quashment of proceedings and for the interest of justice, this point should be addressed in order to avoid conflicting opinions.

3. Civil Appeal No. 11 of 2011 arose from the judgment and order of a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 7610 of 2008 which was instituted by Bo-sun Park and two others (the appellants) challenging the proceedings in GR Case No. 915 of 2008 arising out of Joydevpur PS Case No. 53 dated 14th August, 2008 Civil Appeal No. 12 of 2011 arose against a judgment and order of a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.  10164 of 2007 moved by the appellants challenging the proceedings in CR Case No. 3518 of 2007 pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. Civil Appeal No. 13 of 2011 arose from a judgment of a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1071 of 2007 moved by the appellants challenging the proceedings in GR Case No. 922 of 2007 arising out of Joydevpur PS Case No. 83 (9) 2007 pending in the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gazipur. Civil Petition No. 1159 of 2011 arose from a judgment and order of a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 10675 of 2007 heard along with Writ Petition No. 719 of 2008 discharging the rules which petitions were filed challenging the proceedings in GR Case No. 746 of 2007 pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. Respondent Ms Ok-Kyung Oh, a South Korean Citizen is the informant in GR Case Nos. 746 of 2007, 915 of 2008 and 922 of 2007, while the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies is the complainant in CR Case No.  3518 of 2007.

4. Short facts relevant for the disposal of the appeals and the petition are as follows:

5. The appellants allegedly in collusion with each others fabricated a number of Board Meetings and Resolutions of Tea-Hung Packaging (BD) Limited, a foreign investment company in Bangladesh in which Bo-Sun Park is the Chairman. The accused-persons manufactured some false and forged documents with a view to prevent the respondent from functioning as the Managing Director of the company when the respondent was away from the country. In GR Case No.  922 of 2007, the respondent alleged that she was the Managing Director of the Company. On 30th June, 2007 the appellants submitted summary of share capital to the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies forging her signature while she was in Korea. The police took up the case for investigation and at this stage, the appellants moved the High Court Division challenging the investigation of the case. In the complaint, the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies alleged that Bo-Sun Park submitted on 6th March, 2004 a list of directors said to have been prepared on 9th February, 2004 showing his resignation as Chairman of the company and appointing him as Managing Director. Subsequently the respondent made a complaint on 4th March, 2005 stating that she did not resign from the office of the Managing Director of the company and that the return was submitted forging her signature. Pursuant to such complaint, the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate issued process against the appellants under section 397 of the Companies Act, 1994.

6. The High Court Division discharged all other rules. In Writ Petition Nos. 7610 of 2008 and 10171 of 2007, the High Court Division observed that the filing of several cases even after submission of final reports by the police is not a ground for quashing a proceeding and that in presence of alternative remedy, the writ petitions are not maintainable. In Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2007 the High Court Division held that the writ petition in presence of alternative remedy is available to the writ petitioners. The High Court Division, however, repelled the contention raised on behalf of the appellants about the maintainability of the complaint observing "the Registrar acted within the four corners of Section 397 by referring to the said annual return on capital in his complaint petition and, hence, it would remain open to the Court below to ascertain through examination of witnesses and evidence, whether the allegation of false statement in the annual return of the company." In Writ Petition No. 10171 of 2007, the High Court Division observed that there are prima facie allegations of forgery against the appellants and that the writ petition challenging the case at the stage of investigation is not maintainable. In other two writ petitions the High Court Division held that the writ petitioners have no locus-standi to challenge the authority of filing an FIR by the informant-respondent against them and that the writ petitions are not maintainable.

7. Respondent contested the matters challenging the maintainability of the writ petitions mainly on three grounds, firstly, that the writ petitions are not maintainable since the writ petitioners have alternative remedy, secondly, as the writ petitioners are fugitive from justice they are not legally entitled to any relief from the Court and thirdly, interference of the proceedings by the High Court Division at the stage of investigation of the cases are not permissible in law.

8. Mr M Amir-ul-Islam argued that over the selfsame incident, the respondent having instituted series of criminal cases against the appellants, the High Court Division ought to have quashed the proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court in exercise of powers under Article 102 read with Article 109 of the Constitution and that as the High Court Division does not normally interfere into proceedings at the stage of investigation under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the writ jurisdiction is the appropriate forum for protecting the fundamental rights, sufferings of reputation and harassment of innocent persons. The respondent appears in person and submits that the offences allegedly committed by the accused being distinct, and committed on different dates, there is no legal bar in filing different cases. She further submits that the writ petitions are not maintainable.

9. The questions which fall for determination in these appeals are:

(a) whether a writ petition for quashment of a criminal proceeding is maintainable in presence of alternative remedy available under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure,

(b) whether a criminal proceeding can be quashed at the stage of investigation by the police, and

(c) whether a fugitive from justice is entitled to any relief from the High Court Division without appearing in the Court below.

10. The appellants moved Writ Petition No. 7610 of 2008 out of which CA No. 11 of 2001 arose without accompanying the order sheet of the case. Thus, it can not be ascertained whether they had appeared before the Court below before moving the petition. The offences alleged in the FIR being cognizable, it is presumed that processes have already been issued against the appellants before moving the petition. In Civil Petition No. 1159 of 2011, the appellants did not enclose the FIR or the order-sheet in GR Case No. 476 of 2007. It appears from the statements of writ petition that the investigating agency have submitted a charge-sheet against the appellants under sections 468, 201, 385, 506 and 509 of the Penal Code showing them as absconders. There is no statement on whether the learned Magistrate has taken cognizance of the offences pursuant to the filing of the charge-sheet. Admittedly, the appellants are fugitive from justice and thus, in view of the settled principles of law, they are not legally entitled to any relief from a Court of law unless they surrender to the jurisdiction of the Court before they seek discretionary relief.

11. This Division in ACC vs Dr HBM Iqbal, 15 BLC (AD) 45 held that a fugitive from justice is not entitled to obtain a judicial order defying the process of the Court. This Division held:

"We cannot conceive of a more flagrant violation of this principle that a convict who seeks the interference of the sovereign to obtain revision of a judicial order must submit to the Court instead of engaging himself in setting that judicial order at naught. It is well settled that when a person seeks remedy from a Court of law, either in writ jurisdiction or criminal appellate, revisional or miscellaneous jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure he ought to submit to the due process of justice. Let it be made clear to him, if it is not already known that the Court would not act in aid of an accused-person who is a fugitive from law and justice."

12. As regards maintainability of the writ petitions in presence of alternative remedy, there are inconsistent opinions of the High Court Division in this regard. One Bench relying upon the case of State of Haryana vs Bhajan Lal, AIR 1992 SC 604, Dhaka Ware House Ltd. vs Assistant Collector, 11 BLD (AD) 227 and some other decisions of this Division held that the writ petitions are not maintainable and another Bench upon consideration of the same set of decisions held that the writ petitions are maintainable. It is desireable that there should be uniformity of opinions of the High Court Division on a point of law on similar facts. In the High Court Division three type of situations may arise; a single Bench; a Division Bench; and a Full Bench decisions. The inter-relationship between them has been explained by Subba Rao, CJ in Subbaravudu vs the State, 1995 ALT 53 (FB) as under:

"A single Judge shall not differ from the judgment of another Judge of the same Court. If he does not agree, he shall refer the matter to a Bench of two Judges. He is bound by the decision of a Divisional Bench exercising appellate jurisdiction. If there is a conflict of Bench decisions he should refer the case to a Bench of two Judges who may refer it to a Full Bench. A single Judge cannot differ from Divisional Bench unless a Full Bench or the Supreme Court has overruled that decision specifically or laid down different laws on the same point. A Divisional Bench must ordinarily respect another Divisional Bench, but if it differs the case shall be referred to a Full Bench."

<u>13. If a Division Bench does not accept as correct the decision on a question of law of another Division Bench, the only right and proper course is for it to refer the matter to a Full Bench. Chapter VII, Rule 1, of the High Court Division Rules provides whenever a Division Court shall differ from any other Division Court upon a point of law or usage having the force of law, the case shall be referred for decision by a Full Bench". The learned Judges should notice that there is nothing in the oath of a Judge entering upon his office which warrants him in ignoring the rule relating to the binding nature of precedents which is uniformly followed. It is, therefore, hoped that the learned Judges of the High Court Division shall follow the rules, the established norms and conventions. Moreover, judicial decision requires the Judges to follow precedents of the Courts of co-ordinate jurisdiction, unless they are manifestly erroneous and mischievous. A decision is binding not because of its conclusions but in regard to its ratio and the principle laid down therein. The term 'ratio' is the rule of principle acted on by the Court. One Bench of the High Court Division has no jurisdiction to sit in judgment on the decision of another Division Bench.</u>

14. Before embarking upon an inquiry as to the correctness of the opinions, let us consider the scope and limitations of powers exercised by the High Court Division under Article 102 and those by the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. Since the appellants challenged the initiation of criminal proceedings pending in criminal courts there is no doubt that the petitioners have moved the petitions under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution. This is also evident from cause title of the petitions, wherein the writ petitioners described the petitions as one under Article 102 (2) of the Constitution.

15. Clause (2) of Article 102 empowers the High Court Division to interfere with any proceeding if it is satisfied that "no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law". Whereas, Article 226 provides that the High Courts can exercise its jurisdiction for enforcement of fundamental rights and including rights in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quowarranto and certiorari in appropriate cases. Thus, under the Indian provision there is no restrictions for the High Courts in India to invoke writ jurisdiction even in presence of equally efficacious remedy in any case of violation of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court of India has also been given similar power, with the exception that under Article 32 the sole object is the enforcement of the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution whereas, under Article 226 the High Courts have been invested with a wider power relating to the enforcement of fundamental rights as well as ordinary legal rights.

16. Mr M Amir-ul-Islam contends that the appellants in fact have invoked their fundamental rights under clause (1) of Article 102 read with Article 109 of the Constitution. I would deal with the point with regard to the powers under Article 109 of the Constitution later on.

17. As regards the submission of the learned counsel that the writ petitioners have invoked fundamental rights under Article 102(1) merits no consideration, firstly because, the appellants have moved the petitions in the High Court Division under Article 102 (2) of the Constitution. Secondly, they have challenged the proceedings in criminal cases in the nature of writ of certiorari. More so, one of the appellants being a citizen of Korea, he is not entitled to all the rights guaranteed in part III of the Constitution which are available to the citizens of Bangladesh. Only rights guaranteed by Articles 31, 32, 33, 34, 35 and 44 are available to him. Article 31 guarantees the protection of law. It has two parts (1) the citizens and the residents of Bangladesh have the inalienable right to be treated in accordance with law, and (ii) no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation of property of any citizen or resident shall be taken away except in accordance with law. The appellants failed to make out any case that they are not treated in accordance with law. Further, the respondent is also a citizen of Korea and thus, the question of discriminatory treatment does not arise at all to the appellants. Article 35 guarantees rights in respect of trial and punishment. No question of improper trial or illegal conviction or torture or cruelty arises at all. The cases have been initiated under the existing laws of the land and the appellants have challenged the proceedings at preliminary stages. So Article 35 is not applicable, and the other provisions are not at all applicable to the appellants.

18. Now turning to the point of maintainability of a writ petition in presence of alternative remedy, in Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh, 44 DLR (AD) 111, it has been argued by Mustafa Kamal, J. that a person in the service of Republic who intends to invoke fundamental rights for challenging the vires of a law may seek his remedy under Article 102(1), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2) of the Constitution. An aggrieved person may, out of desperation or just for taking a sportive chance in the summary writ jurisdiction, allege contravention of some fundamental rights which may turn out to be frivolous and vextious or not even remotely attracted in his case. The Court is, however, to be "on guard so the great value of the right given under Article 102(1) is not frittered away or misused as a substitute for more appropriate remedy available for an unlawful action involving no infringement of any fundamental right", Mostafa Kamal J observed.

<u>19. In Bangladesh vs Iqbal Hasan Mahmud alias Iqbal Hasan Mahmood Tuku, 60 DLR (AD) 147, this Division approved the views taken in MA Hai vs Trading Corporation of Bangladesh, 40 DLR(AD) 206 and Nasar Ahmed vs Bangladesh, 49 DLR(AD) 111 observing, the contention raised by the learned Attorney-General that writ petition filed by the respondent challenging the proceeding in the aforesaid special case is not maintainable for not having exhausted the otherwise efficacious alternative remedy under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not acceptable, inasmuch as, the instant writ petition has raised question of law and interpretation of statute". This Division though noticed the arguments made by the High Court Division in Jahangir Hossain Howlader vs CMM, Dhaka, 58 DLR 106, did not express any opinion as to the correctness of the opinion expressed by the High Court Division but from the latter observations, such as, "availability of alternative remedy by way of appeal or revision will not stand on the way when the question of law and interpretation of statute is involved" there is no doubt that this Division did not approve the said opinion of the High Court Division and approved the views taken in Mujibur Rahman (Supra). The consistent view of this Division is that even in presence of alternative remedy, the High Court Division can invoke the power of writ jurisdiction if the aggrieved person challenges the vires of a statute which requires interpretation of such statute. The appellants did not challenge the vires of any statute in any of the writ petitions.</u>

20. In Imtiaz Ahmed vs Ghulam Ali, 15 DLR (SC) 283, Fazle Akbar J speaking for the Supreme Court observed that where a right or liability is created by a statute which gives a special remedy for enforcing it the remedies provided by that statute must be availed of. In Dhaka Ware House Limited vs Assistant Collector of Customs (1991) 11 BLD (AD) 227, the writ petitioners challenged demand notices issued by the Assistant Collector of Customs under section 111 of the Customs Act, 1969. In the notices it were alleged that the writ petitioners improperly removed goods from their respective ware-houses and asked them to pay duties. They unsuccessfully challenged the notices before the appellate authority and then moved the High Court Division. In the facts of the case MH Rahman J observed:

"In principle, where an alternative statutory remedy is available, an application under Article 102 may not be entertained to circumvent a statutory procedure. There are, however, exceptions to the rule. Without attempting an exhaustive enumeration of all possible extra-ordinary situations we may note a few of them. Inspite of an alternative statutory remedy, an aggrieved person may take recourse to Article 102 of the Constitution where the vires of a statute or a statutory provision is challenged, where the alternative remedy is not efficacious or adequate, and, where the wrong complained of is so inextricably mixed up that the High Court Division may, for the prevention of public injury and the vindication of public justice, examine that complaint. It is needless to add that the High Court Division is to see that the aggrieved person must have good reason for by passing an alternative remedy."

21. In Collector of Customs vs A Hannan, 42 DLR (AD) 167, the facts of the case were that there was scarcity of sugar in the country in 1984. Government decided to import sugar under Wage Earners' scheme and decided that all registered importers having valid Import Registration Certificates renewed up to date shall be eligible to open Letter of Credit for import of sugar which could be opened upto November 1984. Confessional rate of customs duty was announced. Writ petitioner imported sugar under the scheme which arrived at Chittagong port on 24th November 1984. In the meantime the confessional rate was withdrawn on 6th November, 1984 by the Government. Writ petitioner contended that the Government is estopped from denying the right that has been vested to him by filing a writ petition and that the alternative remedy given under section 194 of the Customs Act is not an equally efficacious remedy because it stipulated deposit of 50% of the amount of Penalty of the duty demanded. At the hearing preliminary objection was raised as to the maintainability of the writ petition in presence of alternative remedy. The High Court Division allowed the writ petition holding that section 30 of the Customs Act was not tenable. This judgment was challenged in this Division and at the hearing some decisions of different jurisdictions were considered.

22. As to the alternative remedy, the contention of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq is fully correct because the remedy provided for in the Act is not equally efficacious remedy to bar the writ jurisdiction', this Division observed. 'The respondent acting upon solemn promise made by the appellant incurred huge expenditure and if the appellant is not held to its promise, the respondent would be put in a very disadvantageous position and, therefore, the principles of promissory estoppel can also be invoked in this case' . It will appear from the above observations that this Division has maintained the judgment of the High Court Division on the doctrine of promissory estoppel, although the maintainability of the writ petition in presence of alternative remedy was also an Issue in the matter.

23. This Division in a later case in Bangladesh vs Mizanur Rahman, 52 DLR (AD) 141, reconsidered the earlier cases on the point of maintainability of writ petition in presence of alternative remedy and observed "Ordinarily writ petition against an order of assessment of customs duty or imposition of fine is not maintainable and remedy of appeal is to be availed of against the same. Holding of petition against order of assessment of customs duty made in the cases of Hannan and Dhaka Warehouse Ltd. should remain confined to the fact of each case and has no universal application in view of the holding in Mohammad Brother's case and the provisions of law and the constitution discussed above." Kazi Ebadul Hoque. J, in his separate opinion observed that a writ petition is filed for enforcement of any fundamental rights under Article 102(1) of the Constitution apparently there is no question of exhaustion of equally efficacious remedy and, as such, in spite of such remedy being available a writ petition for enforcement of any fundamental rights appears to be maintainable when fundamental rights is sought to be enforced only to avail and the alternative remedy available under the law unless vires of the law is challenged. However, when a writ petition is filed under Article 102(2) of the Constitution the question of exhaustion of other equally efficacious remedy arises. If any law provides for any remedy to any wrong done in respect of anything in exercise of power under that law by creating a forum ordinarily that remedy is to be availed of by the aggrieved person.

24. In Mohammad Brothers vs Collector of Customs, 48 DLR (AD) 58, this Division held that the writ petition challenging the order of assessment of customs duty was not maintainable as Customs Act provided remedy against the same by appeal and revision. The views taken in Mizanur Rahman have been approved in Collector of Customs vs AKM Salauddin, 60 DLR (AD) 71.

25. In CA Abraham vs Income Tax Officer, AIR 1961 SC 609, the question was whether in presence of alternative remedy available under the Income Tax Act, a writ petition under Article 226 of Constitution is maintainable. It has been held by the Supreme Court, the Income Tax Act provides a complete machinery for assessment of tax and imposition of penalty and for obtaining relief in respect of any improper orders passed by the Income Tax Authorities and the aggrieved person could not be permitted to abandon resort to that machinery and to invoke the writ jurisdiction of the High Court when he had adequate remedy open to him by an appeal to the Tribunal.

26. In State of Himachal Pradesh vs Raja Mahendra Pal, AIR 1999 SC 1786, a Maharaja of Himachal claimed relief in the High Court for issuance of the command to the State Forest Corporation by treating him equivalent to the Government of Himachal Pradesh with conferment of monetary grants. The High Court gave him the relief. The Supreme Court held that the right of the Maharaja, if any, are based upon a contract for which he was obliged to avail of by way of "the alternative efficacious remedy for filing a suit either for recovery of the money or for ambition of a grounds. The alternative remedy available to the Maharaja admittedly not being efficacious he could not maintain a petition for writ". As observed above, the Indian Provision in Article 226 does not contain the expression alternative efficacious remedy' as is used in our provision, even then, the Indian Supreme Court's stand is, in presence of 'alternative remedy' or 'adequate remedy' the power of judicial review in exercise of discretionary power in writ jurisdiction is not permissible.

27. Learned counsel has stressed upon the case of Jahangir Hossain Howlader vs CMM, Dhaka, 58 DLR 106, in which, the accused filed a writ petition challenging a criminal proceeding. The State opposed the rule on the ground that in presence of alternative remedy under section 561A the writ petition was not maintainable. The High Court Division relying upon the cases of State of Haryana vs Bhajan LAI, AIR 1992 SC 604, Messrs Pepsi Food Limited vs Special Judicial Magistrate AIR 1998 SC 128, and state of WBV Swapan Kumar Guha, AIR 1982 SC 949, observed that filing of an application under section 561A is not an adequate remedy and that writ jurisdiction is available for quashing a proceeding in order to prevent abuse of the process of the Court. In that case the petitioner did not challenge the vires of any statute, he had challenged the proceedings of a criminal case. Now the question is whether, the High Court Division in Jahangir Hossain is justified in quashing the proceedings of a criminal case in writ jurisdiction following the Indian decisions and whether, the High Court Division has properly appreciated the ratio decidendi in those cases.

28. In the case of Pepsi Food Limited, accused being unsuccessful in the Lucknow Bench of the Allahabad High Court to quash the proceeding by filing a writ petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution moved the Supreme Court of India. There was allegation that the accused-persons by selling, distributing, manufacturing and marketing adulterated and harmful for health 'Lehar Pepsi' have committed an offence under section 7(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The Supreme Court on perusal of the complaint found that the allegations against the accused did not make out any case under section 7 of the Act and that there is no basis for the complainant to make such complaint. The Supreme Court then accepted one of the guide-lines formulated in Bhajan Lars case and observed, "certainly one of those cases where there is an abuse of the process of the law and the Courts and the High Court should not have shied away in exercising its jurisdiction". The Supreme Court observed that in Bhajan Lal's case, one of the guidelines was that where the allegations made in the first information report or the complaint even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence, interference is justified. The powers conferred upon the High Court under Article 227 have no limit but more the power, more due care and caution is to be exercised invoking this power. The Supreme Court noticed that the power can be exercised under Article 482 but the accused chose to invoke power under Articles 226 and 227. The Supreme Court then concluded its arguments observing that nomenclature under which petition is filed is not quite relevant and that does not debar the Court from exercising its jurisdiction which otherwise it possesses unless there is special procedure prescribed which procedure is mandatory. If in a case like the present one the Court finds that the appellants could not invoke its jurisdiction under Article 226, the Court can certainly treat the petition as one under Article 227 or Section 482 of the Code. It may not, however, be lost sight of that provisions exist in the Code of revision and appeal but sometimes for immediate relief Section 482 of the Code or Article 227 may have to be resorted to for correcting some grave errors that might be committed by the sub-ordinate Courts. The present petition though filed in the High Court as one under Articles 226 and 227 could well be treated under Article 227 of the Constitution" the Supreme Court said.

29. In Babhutmal Raichand Oswal vs Laxmibai R Tarte, AIR 1975 SC 1297, it was observed that the jurisdiction under Article 227 could not be exercised "as the cloak of an appeal in disguise. It does not lie in order to bring up an order or decision for rehearing the issues raised in the proceedings". The High Court Division in Jahangir Hossain Hawlader's case failed to follow the ratio decidendi of Pepsi Food Limited's case. The Supreme Court interfered with the proceeding on being satisfied that even on admitted facts disclosed in the complaint no offence disclosed at all and exercised its power under Article 227 of the Constitution.

<u>30. The consistent views of this Division are that if any alternative remedy is available, the judicial review by the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction is not available with the exception that where the vires of a statutory provision is challenged or where the alternative remedy is not efficacious exercise of such power may be justified. The High Court Division in Jahangir Hossain observed that before moving a petition under section 561A of the Code, the petitioner is required to surrender before the Court below and thus the filing of a petition under section 561A is not an adequate remedy. There is falacy in the arguments for, the High Court Division failed to address the point in the light of the decisions of this Division. If a process has already been issued against an accused, the High Court Division shall not exercise its power either in writ or revisional or miscellaneous jurisdictions unless he surrenders to the jurisdiction of the Court. Article 102 does not confer any wider power to circumvent the statutory procedure.</u>

31. In Bhajan Lal's case, the respondent Bhajan Lal challenged the initiation of the criminal proceeding in question by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the nature of a writ of certiorari for quashing the first information report and also in the nature of a writ of prohibition for restraining from proceeding with the investigation of the case. The incident in question arose over an election related dispute. The High Court of Haryana came to the conclusion that the allegations made in the FIR are imaginary and fantastic that the sole object of the complainant was to set the machinery of the criminal law in motion against the respondent Bhajan Lal, that the charges levelled against accused are groundless and that the allegations do not constitute a cognizable offence for commencing the lawful investigation. The Supreme Court of India upon consideration of all previous decisions on the point of High Court's power to quash a criminal proceeding during pendency of investigation formulated 7 categories of cases in which interference may be justified. It has been observed that the High Courts in exercise of powers under Article 226 of the Constitution or under section 482 corresponding to section 561A of our Code of Criminal Procedure can exercise its power to prevent abuse of the process of the Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The Supreme Court however, did not approve the High Court's view and observed "the complaint shall not be thrown over-board on the mere unsubstantiated plea of malafides." The Supreme Court set-aside the judgment of the High Court with a strong note of disapproval in the manner the High Court quashed the FIR, observing:

"Here we are constrained to express our disapproval since the text, tenor and tone of the above observations leave us with the feeling that such misplaced sympathy indicated therein appears to have considerably weighed with the learned Judges in taking extreme step in quashing the First Information Report."

32. The Supreme Court noticed that the officer investigating the offences was not clothed with the authority to investigate the offences and accordingly observed that the State Government, if so desired, can direct an investigation "through a competent police officer empowered with valid legal authority "

33. The High Court Division reproduced those 7 categories of cases formulated in Bhajan Lal's case and one Bench said that those categories do not attract the appellants' cases, the other Bench without expressing any opinion came to the conclusion that it has power to exercise the writ jurisdiction to quash a criminal proceeding. Mr M Amir-ul-Islam failed to appreciate the ratio decidendi in Bhajan Lars case and submitted with circumlocution that since the FIRs and the complaint were made against the appellants with malafide motive to humiliate and persecute the appellants, on the principles argued in Bhajan Lal, the proceedings are liable to be quashed. Learned counsel failed to notice that none of the guidelines formulated in Bhajan Lal is applicable in these cases. Secondly, those guidelines are in the nature of obiter dictum and the Supreme Court did not follow those guide lines while interfering with the judgment of the High Court.

<u>34. In State of Bihar vs JAC Saldanha (1980) 1 SCC 554, the Supreme Court of India approved its earlier opinions and observed that the Court disapproved the exercise of the extraordinary power of the High Courts in issuing prerogative writs quashing the prosecution solely on the basis of averments in affidavit. I respectfully endorse the above view and observe that an FIR or a complaint should not be thrown overboard merely on the basis of the submission of the learned Counsel or on the basis of statements in the petitions that the cases have been instituted to persecute the accused with malafide intention. The submissions that the cases have been instituted malafide or to persecute the accused-persons are disputed facts which can not be looked into and decided in a summary petition exercising extra-ordinary powers and generally not reviewable. In exercising the power of judicial review the High Court Division does not assume the function of an appellate authority. Article 102(2) (a)(ii) empowers the High Court Division to issue an order declaring an act done or proceeding taken to be without lawful authority or where there is an error apparent on the face of the record or in cases where the person proceeded against has committed an error going to jurisdiction i.e. when the act done or proceeding taken is vitiated by lack of jurisdiction or by being in excess of jurisdiction.</u>

35. If the allegations in the first information report disclose a cognizable offence, an Officer-in-Charge of a police station on being satisfied about the requirement of section 154(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure has no option other than to enter the substance thereof in the prescribed form and investigate upon the allegations for ascertaining the truth or falsehood of the allegations under Chapter XIV of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The condition precedent to the investigation under section 157(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is the existence of the reason to suspect the commission of a cognizable offence which has to be disclosed in the first information report. No court has any power to interfere with such investigation, inasmuch as, the powers and functions of the Court and the investigating agency are complementary. In Bhajan Lal's case the Supreme Court approved the arguments of Privy Council in Emperor vs Khawaja Nazir Ahmed, AIR 1945 PC 18 and some other decisions on the point of the power of a police officer in the field of investigation of a cognizable offence and observed in paragraph 62 as under:

"The sum and substance of the above deliberation results to a conclusion that the investigation of an offence is the field exclusively reserved for the police officers whose powers in that field are unfettered so long as the power to investigate into the cognizable offences is legitimately exercised in strict compliance with the provisions falling under Chapter XII of the Code and the Courts are not justified in obliterating the track of investigation when the investigating agencies are well within their legal bounds as aforementioned. Indeed, a noticeable feature of the scheme under Chapter XIV of the Code is that a Magistrate is kept in the picture at all stages of the police investigation but he is not authorised to interfere with the actual investigation or to direct the police how that investigation is to be conducted. But if a police officer transgresses the circumscribed limits and improperly and illegally exercises his investigatory powers in breach of any statutory provision causing serious prejudice to the personal liberty and also property of a citizen, then the Court on being approached by the person aggrieved for the redress of any grievance has to consider the nature and extent of the breach and pass appropriate orders as may be called for without leaving the citizens to the mercy of police echelons since human dignity is a dear value of our Constitution. Needs no emphasis that no one can demand absolute immunity even if he is wrong and claim unquestionable right and unlimited powers exercisable up to unfathomable cosmos. Any recognition of such power will be tantamount to recognition of Divine Power which no authority on earth can enjoy."

36. In Abhinandan Jha vs Dinesh Mishra, AIR 1968 SC 117, while approving the views of Nazir Ahmed and some other decisions, the Supreme Court of India explained the power of the Court and the investigating agency in a criminal proceeding that the investigation, under the Code, takes in several aspects, and stages, ending ultimately with the formation of an opinion by the police as to whether, on the materials covered and collected a case is made out to place the accused before the Magistrate for trial, and the submission of either a charge-sheet, or a final report is dependent on the nature of the opinion, so formed. The formation of the said opinion, by the police, as pointed out earlier, is the final step in the investigation, and that final step is to be taken only by the police and by no other authority.

37. In State of Bihar vs AC Saldana, AIR 1980 SC 326, it is stated that investigation of an offence is the field exclusively reserved for the executive through the police department, the superintendence over which vests in the government. The executive which is charged with a duty to keep vigilance over law and order situation is obliged to prevent crime and if an offence is alleged to have been committed it is its bounden duty to investigate into the offence and bring the offender to book. Once it investigates and finds an offence having been committed, it is its duty to collect evidence for the purpose of proving the offence. Once that is complete and the investigating agency submits report to the Court to take cognizance its duty comes to an end. There is thus a well defined and demarcated function in the field of crime detection and its adjudication between the police and the Court. The Supreme Court approved the views taken in the case of Nazir Ahmed. The Supreme Court disapproved the High Court's interference by exercising the power by writ of mandamus to close the case before the investigation is complete.

38. In Madhavrao vs Sambhajirao, AIR 1988 SC 709, it was observed that when a prosecution at initial stage is asked to be quashed, the test to be applied by the Court is whether the uncontroverted allegations prima-facie establish the offence. It is for the Court to take into consideration any special features which appear in a particular case to consider whether it is expedient and in the interest of justice to permit a prosecution to continue. This is on the basis that the Court can not be utilized for any oblique purpose and where in the opinion of the Court chances of an ultimate conviction are bleak and, no useful purpose is likely to be served by allowing a criminal prosecution to continue, the Court may while taking into consideration the special facts of a case also quash the proceeding even though it may be at a preliminary stage.

39. In Lal Mandi vs State of WB (1995) 3 SCC 601, the Supreme Court of India held:

"ordinarily the Court should refrain from interfering at a premature stage of the investigation as that may derail the investigation and the demoralize investigation. Of late, the tendency to interfere in the investigation is on the increase and courts should be weary of its possible consequences".

40. In a later case, in State of Himachal Pradesh vs Shri Pirthi Chand, AIR 1996 SC 977, the Supreme Court considered the arguments made in the case of Bhajan Lal and came to the conclusion that the guidelines given therein were "illustrative". It was observed, the High Courts should sparingly and only in exceptional cases, in rarest of rare cases, and not merely it would be appealable to the Court be inclined to exercise power. The Supreme Court clarified the expression "rarest of rare cases" by observing that, the Court first has to get into the grip of the matter whether the allegations constitute the offence. The Supreme Court cautioned that FIR being an initiation to move the machinery into action, after investigation is concluded and the police report is filed, the prosecution produces the statements of the witnesses in support of the charge-sheet. At that stage it is not the function of the Court to weigh the pros and cons of the prosecution case or to consider necessity of strict compliance of the provisions which are considered mandatory. This would be done after the trial is concluded. The Court concluded its arguments observing that the remedy under section 482(561A) is available when

"the High Court would be loath and circumspect to exercise its extra-ordinary power under Article 226 since efficacious remedy under section 482 of the Code is available. When the Court exercises its inherent power under section 482 the prime consideration should only be whether the exercise of the power would advance the cause of Justice or it would be an abuse of the process of the Court.... The social stability and order requires to be regulated by proceeding against the offender as it is an offence against the society as a whole. This cardinal principle should always be kept in mind before embarking upon exercising inherent power".

41. In another case in State of Kerala vs OC Kuttan, AIR 1999 SC 1044, the High Court of Kerala in exercise of extra-ordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution quashed the criminal proceedings against five accused-persons on the reasonings that the uncontroverted allegations made in the first information report and other statements do not constitute the offence of rape. On appeal from the said judgment, the Supreme Court considered the cases of Bhajan Lal and Sanchaita Investment and expressed similar views that the guidelines given in the case of Bhajan Lal were "by way of illustrations though on facts it was held that the High Court was not justified in quashing the first information report". The Supreme Court noticed the note of caution given in Bhajan Lal that "the power of quashing the criminal proceedings should be exercised very sparingly with circumspection and that too in the rarest of rare cases, that the court will not be justified in embarking upon an inquiry as to the reliability or genuineness or otherwise of the allegations made in the FIR or the complaint and that the extra-ordinary or inherent powers do not confer an arbitrary jurisdiction on the Court to act according to its whim or caprice". The Court reiterated its earlier opinions that the first information report is only an initiation to move the machinery to investigate into the offence and, therefore, while exercising the power and deciding whether the investigation itself should be quashed, utmost care should be taken by the Court and at that stage it is not possible for the Court to sift the materials or to weigh the materials and then come to the conclusion one way or the other. The Supreme Court set-aside the judgment of the High Court and directed the investigating agency to proceed with the investigation.

42. The Supreme Court of Pakistan and this Division took similar views. In Government of Bangladesh vs AT Mridha, 26 DLR (SC) 17, the powers of the High Court Division to quash a proceeding under section 561A has been exhaustively considered. In that case the views taken in Nazir Ahmed and the Supreme Courts of Pakistan and India were considered. MA Jabir J speaking for the Supreme Court after reiterating all the earlier decisions of the apex Courts of the sub-continent concluded as under:

"The power vested under section 561A of the Code can be exercised for the purposes specified therein, namely, (a) to give effect to any order under the Code or (b) to prevent abuse of the process of any Court, or (c) to secure the ends of justice. The tendency to invoke this section, not infrequently, upon an assumption that it gives some new or increased powers to the High Court, appears to persist even though it has repeatedly been pointed out that such assumption is not correct It merely safeguards all existing inherent powers possessed by a High Court necessary (among other purposes) to secure the ends of justice".

43. While endorsing Nazir Ahmed's case it has been observed, there might be good reason for the High Court to interfere with the proceedings at the initial stage but the statutory right of the police to investigate the circumstances of an alleged cognizeable offence without requiring any authority from judicial authorities and it would be an unfortunate result "if it should be held to be possible to interfere with these statutory rights by any exercise of inherent jurisdiction of the Court".

44. The above arguments have been approved by this Division in Bangladesh vs Tan Kheng Hock, 31 DLR (AD) 69. In that case though police submitted a charge-sheet against the accused but before the Court takes cognizance, the accused moved the High Court Division for quashing the proceedings. The accused took the plea that the charge-sheet was submitted before the Sub-Divisional Magistrate who was not competent to take cognizance of the offence punishable under section 25B of the Special Powers Act. The question considered in that case was whether the High Court Division was justified in quashing the proceeding at that stage. This Division was of the view that this interference amounted to practically quashing the charge-sheet because pursuant to filing of the charge-sheet no step in the proceeding was taken. The High Court Division is not given unrestricted and undefined power to make any order under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court Division cannot exercise its inherent power unless it is absolutely necessary for carrying out the other provisions of the Code or for doing justice, i.e. to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. With these findings, this Division interfered with the judgment of the High Court Division and directed to continue with the case in accordance with law observing:

"Section 561A emphasizes that the High Court has the jurisdiction to pass orders to secure the ends of justice and for that purpose the High Court is competent to entertain applications not provided by the Code. However, it must be clearly understood that the terms of section 561A of the Code do not extend the jurisdiction of the High Court to matters which are not inherently with that jurisdiction. The High Court also cannot claim inherent jurisdiction to exercise powers taken away by legislation. When exercising this jurisdiction, the High Court would not embark upon an enquiry whether the evidence in question is reliable or not. This is the function of the trial Magistrate and it might so happen that quashment of a criminal proceedings before commencement of trial would amount to stifling the proceedings before the prosecution got an opportunity to bring evidence in support of the accusation. That is why their Lordships of the Judicial Committee in the case of Emperor vs Nazir Ahmad expressed a word of caution that the Court might be acting on treacherous grounds in quashing criminal proceedings at the interlocutory stage or at the early stage on the ground that continuation of the proceedings would be an abuse of the process of the Court. We fully agree with the view taken by their Lordships of the Judicial Committee that the extra-ordinary power of the Court under section 561A should be exercised very cautiously to avoid miscarriage of justice."

45. In Nasiruddin Mahmud vs Momtazuddin Ahmed 36 DLR (AD) 14, Sahabuddin Ahmed J expressing the minority views explained the arguments made in Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State, 28 DLR (AD) 39 that "interference even at an initial stage may be justified". It is observed 'initial stage' does not mean any stage prior to submission of charge-sheet by the police but it means a stage after submission of the charge-sheet. The majority opinion is of course in favour of quashing the proceedings on taking into consideration that the allegations made in the complaint do not disclose an offence. In that case a complaint was made on the allegation that the accused borrowed from time to time from the complainant some money for the purpose of their business. One accused issued two cheques for repayment which were dishonoured. The complainant admitted that the accused agreed to work as partners but in due course the accused No. 1 misappropriated money of the firm by various means. BH Chowdhury, J speaking for the majority approved the views taken in Bhuban Mohan vs Surendra Das, AIR 1951 Cal 69 (FB) that "the working partner is authorised to recover the dues of the partnership and to spend the money for the business of partnership, he cannot be said to have been guilty of criminal breach of trust even with respect to the dues realised  " inasmuch as, in a partnership business there cannot be any entrustment of any property by one partner to the other within the meaning of section 405 of the Penal Code.

46. In Md Shamsuddin alias Lambu vs State, 40 DLR (AD) 69, the minority opinion of Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J is that when a case is launched from an improper motive only to harass the accused due to personal vendetta, the Court should exercise such jurisdiction which has been given power to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court. The majority view is that this is not a legal ground for quashing a proceeding. It is argued by majority that it is for the prosecution to prove the case on evidence and the power may be exercised only in those cases which are not covered by any specific provision of the Code. The inherent power must be exercised very sparingly and with great caution.

47. In Hussain Mohammad Ershad vs The State, 43 DLR (AD) 50, the petitioner moved a petition under section 561A in the High Court Division on the ground amongst others that the proceeding was instituted for malafide purpose as per order of the Ministry of Home Affairs. This Division repelled the contention on the reasoning that this is not a legal ground for quashing a criminal proceeding. This Division has echoed the views taken in Bhajan Lal that on the plea of malafide a complaint or an FIR should not be thrown out in exercise of inherent power.

48. In Al-haj Md Serajuddowlah vs State, 43 DLR (AD) 198, it is observed

"the High Court Division will be loath to stifle a prosecution at the initial stage of the proceeding unless the facts of the case are apparently and clearly such as would attract an invariable inference that even upon the admitted facts no case as alleged or as may be alleged under any penal law can be made out and that further continuation of the proceeding would be an abuse of the process of the Court".

49. Thus a proceeding cannot be quashed merely on the ground that it has been initiated for malafide or oblique purposes for humiliating the accused or that it has been initiated from an improper motive or to harass the accused due to personal vendatta under section 561A or Article 102. Section 561A or Article 102 does not invest any increased power to the High Court Division. The Supreme Court of India in Shri Pirthi Chand (AIR 1996 SC 977) expressed similar language as has been expressed by this Division.

50. Now turning to the case of state of West Bengal vs Swapan Kumar Guha, AIR 1982 SC 949, the facts are that a partnership firm carried on the business of financiers and investors and in the business the firm accepted loans or deposits from the general public. Under the terms and conditions of deposits, the firm has also liberty to repay the amount with interest to any depositor before expiry of the statutory period. Later on the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Schemes (Banking) Act, 1978 was promulgated. The Bureau of Investigation made a complaint against the firm and its partners for violation of the Act of 1978. Two partners were arrested and various documents were seized from the office of the firm. Those arrestees filed a writ petition challenging the validity of the FIR and proceedings including the validity of searches and seizures. It is claimed that the allegations in the FIR even if they are taken to be correct, there cannot be any question of any violation of the Act and no offence under the Act is disclosed. The High Court quashed the proceeding and the FIR. The Supreme Court was of the opinion that the materials do not indicate anything to disclose that the firm is promoting or conducting any 'Prize Chit' defined in section 2(e) of the Act, and that the firm indulges in high risk investments and advances monies which acts are neither illegal nor the firm makes easy or quick money. The Court thereupon concluded its opinion as under:

"The legal position appear to be that if an offence is disclosed, the Court will not normally interfere with an investigation into the case and will permit investigation into the offence alleged to be completed: if, however, the materials do not disclose an offence, no investigation should normally be permitted as any investigation, in the absence of any offence being disclosed, will result in unnecessary harassment to a party, whose liberty and property may be put to jeopardy for nothing  If the Court interferes with the power of investigation in a case where an offence has been disclosed, the offence will be unpunished to the serious detriment of the welfare of the society and the cause of justice suffers. It is on the basis of this principle that the Court normally does not interfere with the investigation of a case where the offence has been disclosed

51. The High Court Division in Jahangir Hossain Howlader has totally overlooked the decisions of this Division and relied upon Swapan Kumar Guha's case. While deciding Swapan Kumar's case, the Supreme Court of India distinguished the views expressed by the Judicial Committee in Nazir Ahmad observing that the right of police of inquiry is 'conditioned by the existence of reason to suspect the commission of cognizable offence and they cannot, reasonably, have reason so to suspect unless the FIR, prima-facie, discloses the commission of such offence." Even then, the Supreme Court refused the prayer for returning the seized documents of the firm observing "The state Government, the Central Government and the Reserve Bank of India must be given a reasonable opportunity to see if it is possible, under the law, to institute an inquiry into the affairs of the firm and, in the meantime, to regulate its affairs." This decision in Swapan Kumar Guha has not been followed by the Supreme Court in latter cases including in Bhajan Lal, in which case, the State Government was afforded liberty, if any, to investigate into the offences by a competent investigating officer.

<u>52. We find from the above discussions that the views expressed by the Judicial Committee in Nazir Ahmed (AIR 1945 PC 18) hold the field till now and the apex Courts of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh have been following the said opinions to great respect. The functions of the judiciary and the police are complementary, not overlapping and the combination of individual's liberty with a due observance of law and order is only to be obtained by leaving each to exercise its own function-the Court's function begins when a charge is preferred before it and not until then and, therefore, the High Court Division can interfere under section 561A only when a charge has been preferred and not before. The interference in exercise of powers under Article 102 has been deprecated on repeated occasions and such exercise of powers is justified only in exceptional cases as observed above.</u>

53. Where the allegations in the FIR or Complaint even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima-facie constitute any offence, or where in the opinion of the Court chances of the ultimate conviction are bleak and no useful purpose is likely to be served by allowing the criminal prosecution, or when the power would advance the cause of justice or it would be an abuse of the process of the Court, interference in such exceptional cases may be justified. This power of the Court does not confer any arbitrary jurisdiction to act according to its whims. The High Court Division would be loath and circumspect to exercise its extra-ordinary power at an initial stage of the proceeding. The Court will not be justified in embarking upon an inquiry as to the reliability or genuiness of the allegations made in the FIR or Complaint.

<u>54. It is noticeable that even in Swapan Kuamar (ibid), the Supreme Court of India while maintaining the High Court's judgment expressed its anxiety to quash the proceeding at the initial stage observing that if the Court interferes with the power of investigation in a case where offence has been disclosed, the offender will be unpunished to the serious detriment of the welfare of the society and the cause of justice suffers. I fully agree with the above opinion. The principle behind it is that the Court normally does not interfere with the investigation of a case where the offence has been disclosed in the FIR or complaint. The tendency of interference at the stage of investigation of a case is now on the rise which has not happened earlier even though it has repeatedly been pointed out that such assumption is not correct. The Courts should be weary of its possible consequence.</u>

<u>55. The submissions that filing of several cases over the self-same allegation even after submission of final report in favour of the accused are abuse of the process of the Court does not merit consideration. The principle of double jeopardy or for that matter, res judicata does not rest on any doctrine of estoppel. The principle is that no person should be vexed with several trials for offences arising out of the identical acts committed by him. When an offence has already been the subject of judicial investigation and adjudication, and there has been an acquittal, the acquittal is conclusive. There is nothing like res judicata in a criminal trial as long as it does not terminate in either acquittal or conviction so as to attract the provisions of section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.</u>

56. The appellants have not been tried by a criminal Court and therefore, continuation of investigation even after submission of final report is not prohibited by law. The only question is whether on the admitted facts, offences alleged under any penal law or any other laws have been made out. The learned counsel did not make any argument by referring to the FIRs and complaint that on the admitted facts no case under any existing provisions of law has been disclosed. Therefore, even the statements of law argued in the case of Swapan Kumar Guha and Bhajan Lal (supra) are not also applicable to these cases. In this connection a dictum of Haisbury in Quinn vs Leathern, 1901 AC 495 deserves mention. "A case is only an authority for what it actually decides." Whenever allegations for commission of offence are disclosed in the FIR or complaint, the quashment of such criminal proceeding before commencement of the trial would amount to stifling the proceedings before the prosecution gets an opportunity to bring evidence in support of the accusation which is not permissible in law.

57. Next point urged by Mr M Amir-ul-Islam is that the High Court Division has power of superintendence and control over all Courts sub-ordinate to it under Article 109 of the Constitution and thus, in appropriate cases, the High Court Division can quash a proceeding if it is found that there is abuse of the process of the Court. This supervisory power of the High court Division, it is argued, is wide enough to interfere with any proceeding in the interest of justice. I fail to understand how this power can be exercised for quashing a criminal proceeding either at the stage of investigation or after taking cognizance of the offence after completion of investigation? Article 109 has not been couched in the similar language of Article 227 of the Indian provision. It would be appropriate if I reproduce the relevant provisions before expressing my opinion on the point raised by the learned counsel. Article 109 of our Constitution reads:

"109. The High Court Division shall have superintendence and control over all courts (and tribunals) sub-ordinate to it."

58. Article 227 of the Indian Constitution provides:

"(1) Every High Court shall have superintendence over all Courts and tribunals throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction.

(2) Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provision, the High Court may—

(a) call for returns from such courts;

(b) make and issue general rules and prescribe forms for regulating the practice and proceedings of such courts; and

(c) prescribe forms in which books, entries and accounts shall be kept by the officers of any such courts.

(3) The High Court may also settle tables of fees to be allowed to the sheriff and all clerks and officers of such courts and to attorneys, advocates and pleaders practicing therein;

59. The language of section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 and section 15 of the High Courts Act, 1861 have been retained in Article 227 except that the power of superintendence has been extended by this article to Tribunals. Section 107 of Act of 1915 has been reproduced in section 224 of the Government of India Act, 1935. In section 224, subsection (2) was added providing that nothing in section 224 should be construed as giving the High Court any jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior Court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. There are opinions of the superior Courts of this sub-continent that the idea was presumably to nullify the effect of the decisions of the High Court. The significant omission has been regarded by the Courts before whom this question has arisen as having restored to the High Court the power of judicial superintendence it had under section 15 of the High Courts Act, 1861 and section 107 of Act of 1915. There is no corresponding provision similar to clause (2) of Article 227 in our Constitution.

60. In Babhutmal vs Laxmibai, AIR 1975 SC 1297, it has been argued that the High Court cannot while exercising jurisdiction under Article 227, interfere with findings of fact recorded by the sub-ordinate Court or Tribunal. Its function is limited to seeing that the sub-ordinate Court or Tribunal functions within the limits of its authority. It cannot correct mere errors of fact by examining the evidence and re-appreciating it. What Morris, LT, said in Rex vs Northumberland Compensation Appeal Tribunal (1952-1 All ER 122) in regard to the scope and ambit of certiorari jurisdiction must apply equally in relation to exercise of jurisdiction under Article 227. That jurisdiction cannot be exercised:

"as the cloak of an appeal in disguise. It does not lie in order to bring up an order or decision for rehearing of the issues raised in the proceedings."

61. If an error of fact, even though apparent on the face of the record, cannot be corrected by means of a writ of certiorari it should follow a fortiori that it is not subject to correction by the High Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 227. The power of superintendence under Article 227 cannot be invoked to correct an error of fact which only a superior court can do in exercise of its statutory power as a court of appeal. The High Court cannot in guise of exercising its jurisdiction under Article 227 convert itself into a court of appeal when the legislature has not conferred a right of appeal and made the decision of the sub-ordinate court or tribunal final on facts."

62. The power of the High Courts under Article 227 of the Constitution has been explained in Satyanarayan vs Mallikarun, AIR 1960 SC 137 by KC Das Gupta J as under:

"Article. 227 corresponds to Section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915. The scope of that section has been discussed in many decisions of Indian High Courts. However wide it may be than the provisions of S.115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it is well established that the High Court cannot in exercise of its power under that section assume appellate powers to correct every mistake of law. Here there is no question of assumption of excessive jurisdiction or refusal of exercise jurisdiction or any irregularity, or illegality in the procedure or any breach of any rule of natural justice. If anything it may merely be an erroneous decision which, the error not being apparent on the face of  the record, cannot be corrected by the High Court in revision under S.115 of the Code of Civil Procedure or under Article 227."

63. In a latter case in Achutananda Baidya vs Profulla Kumar Gayen, AIR 1997 SC 2077, the scope of the High Courts to interfere with the judgment of the High Courts in exercise of its power of superintendence has been explained by GN Ray, J. It has been observed that the power of superintendence of the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution is not confined to administrative superintendence only but such power includes within its sweep the power of judicial review. The power and duty of the High Court under Article 227 is essentially to ensure that the Courts and Tribunals, inferior to High Court, have done what they were required to, do. Law is well settled by various decisions of this Court that the High Court can interfere under Article 227 of the Constitution in cases of erroneous assumption or acting beyond its jurisdiction, refusal to exercise jurisdiction, error of law apparent on record as distinguished from a mere mistake of law, arbitrary or capricious exercise of authority or discretion, a patent error in procedure, arriving at a finding which is perverse or based on no material, or resulting in manifest injustice. "As regards finding of fact of the inferior Court, the High Court should not quash the judgment of the sub-ordinate Court merely on the ground that its finding of fact was erroneous but it will be open to the High Court in exercise of the powers under Article 227 to interfere with the finding of fact if the sub-ordinate Court came to the conclusion without any evidence or upon manifest misreading of the evidence thereby indulging in improper exercise of jurisdiction or if its conclusions are perverse", the Supreme Court observed.

<u>64. But in respect of powers conferred by Article 109 to the High Court Division is confined to administrative superintendence only; it does not include the power of judicial review or the powers for issuing writ of certiorari. The powers involve a duty on the High Court Division to keep the inferior Courts and Tribunals within the bounds of their authority. This Division in Harun-or-Rashid vs Pubali Bank 60 DLR (AD) 18, considered the scope of Article 109 and observed that Article 109 of the Constitution confers administrative control and supervisory jurisdiction on the High Court Division. The power of control and superintendence is in addition to the power conferred upon the High Court Division to control inferior courts or tribunals through writs under Article 102. Supervisory jurisdiction extends to keeping the sub-ordinate courts and tribunals within the limits of their authority ensuring that they obey law.</u>

<u>65. The relevant arguments are as under:</u>

<u>"This power of superintendence can be exercised where no appeal or revision lies. Power of superintendence and control over the sub-ordinate courts and tribunals under Article 109 is to be exercised sparingly in appropriate cases to keep the sub-ordinate courts within the bounds of their authority and not for correcting mere errors. The power under Article 102 will only be exercised where the party affected moves the court but the power under Article 109 can be exercised by the High Court Division itself. The power of control and superintendence conferred on the High Court Division under Article 109 in relation to sub-ordinate courts or tribunals is administrative in nature. Judicial power of review of the High Court Division can be exercised under Article 102 of the Constitution even in respect of some matter arising out of the supervisory power of the High Court Division under Article 109, inasmuch as, Article 109 is not an enabling Article".</u>

66. What's more, the question of erroneous assumption of power or acting beyond jurisdiction or refusal to exercise jurisdiction by the Courts below does not arise in these cases. The appellants want to quash the proceedings of some criminal cases pending investigation by the police and in some cases the police reports have been filed. Before the Courts give any decision, the appellants wanted to stifle the proceedings. There is therefore, no scope for the High Court Division to exercise its power under Article 109, more so, this point has not been raised and agitated in the High Court Division.

67. The case of Pepsi Co Food Limited (AIR 1998 SC 128) is quite distinguishable and the statement of law argued in that case is not applicable on two grounds; firstly, the Supreme Court considered the power of superintendence of the High Courts under Article 227 of the Constitution and that power must have been resorted to for correcting grave errors that might have been committed by sub-ordinate Courts. The question of correction of errors does not arise in these cases since the writ petitioners have challenged the proceedings at initial stages. Secondly, in that case the Supreme Court did not consider its earlier decisions on the point as to whether in presence of alternative remedy, the aggrieved person can resort to writ jurisdiction. Learned counsel has referred some other decisions which are not at all applicable in the facts and circumstances of the cases and accordingly, I refrain from referring them.

68. In GR. Case No. 746 of 2007 out of which Civil Petition No. 1159 of 2011 and GR Case No. 1915 of 2008 out of which Civil Appeal No. 11 of 2011 arose, there are allegations of forgery and other offences against the accused-persons. The cases are under investigation and the appellants did not enclose the order-sheet and moved the petition enclosing the FIR. An FIR, cannot be taken as a proceeding of the case. Though the appellants gave the corresponding GR Case numbers but I failed to understand why they did not enclose the order-sheets of the cases. In view of the above, the High Court Division has rightly found that the offence complained of in the cases being non-cognizeable offences, the investigation of the cases cannot be challenged by resorting to writ jurisdiction. I find no illegality in the judgment of the High Court Division.

69. In Civil Appeal No. 12 of 2003, the appellants did not enclose the complaint petition. They, however, reproduced the allegations of the complaint in paragraph 3 of the writ petition in which there are allegations of forgery of documents. The learned Magistrate took cognizance of an offence under section 397 of the Companies Act against the appellants. Learned counsel did not make any submission touching to the merit of the case on whether the allegations in the complaint disclose an offence under section 397 of the Companies Act. The High Court Division, in the premises, legally discharged the rule but in the body of the judgment the High Court Division observed "the Registrar's action in including the said allegedly forged resignation letter in the complaint petition, went far beyond what section 397 contemplates". These observations are inconsistent with the operating portion of the judgment. The High Court Division lost sight of the fact that the substance of the allegations in the complaint petition is forgery of the signature. Section 397 is a penal provision for falsifying statement of the company. If those observations remain in the judgment, the trial Court will not be able to adjudicate upon all the points involve in the case independently. Accordingly those observations are expunged.

70. In Civil Appeal No. 13 of 2011, there is also allegation of forgery against the appellants. The appellants moved the writ petition challenging the investigation of the case. The High Court Division on taking into consideration of this aspect discharged the rule on the findings that the writ petition challenging the investigation of a criminal case is not maintainable. I find no illegality in the finding of the High Court Division.

71. In view of the above, the High Court Division is completely justified discharging the rules. The writ petitions challenging the initiation of the criminal proceedings in presence of alternative remedy are not maintainable.
