"Issue a Rule Nisi calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the proceedings in GR Case No. 476/2007 arising out of Motijheel Police Station Case No. 86/660 initiated vide FIR dated 19-7-2007 followed by the charge-sheet No. 723 dated 4-12-2007 should not be declared as malafide and illegal (sic) why the same should not quashed as being initiated with-out any lawful authority and is of no legal effect."

94. But the Rule was issued in a modified form calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why proceedings of the said GR Case initiated vide FIR dated 19-7-2007 fol-lowed by charge-sheet No. 723 dated 4-12-2007 should not be declared to have been made with-out lawful authority and is of no legal effect. A Division Bench of the High Court Division after hearing the said writ petition along with Writ Petition No. 719 of 2008 discharged the Rule on the ground of maintainability; hence the leave petition.

95. Mr M Amir-ul-Islam, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants in all 3(three) appeals as well as in the petition for leave to appeal made submissions elaborating the points on which leave has been granted in 3 (three) leave petitions as quoted hereinbefore. He referred to the FIR and the petition of com-plaint of the earlier cases lodged and filed by respondent No. 3, besides the cases involved in Civil Appeal Nos. 11 and 13 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.  1159 of 2011 and submitted that the instant cases are nothing but harassing filed with malafide motive and are being proceeded with by abusing the process of law and the Court, so the petitioners had /have every right to invoke the special original jurisdiction of the High Court Division under article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (the Constitution), consequently Writ Petition Nos. 7610 of 2008, 10171 of 2007 and 10675 of 2007 were quite maintainable in law, but the High Court Division on an erroneous approach of the concept of availability of the alternative efficacious remedy provided in the Code for the redress of the grievance of the petitioners held that the writ petitions were not maintainable and thus, fell into an error in dis-charging the Rules. He further argued that constitutional concept of protecting a citizen from being harassed unnecessarily and in a malafide manner by filing series of false cases over the selfsame allegations cannot override the procedural law as provided in the Code, the High Court Division erred in law in not setting—aside/quashing the respective criminal proceeding challenged in 3(three) writ petitions. In support of his contentions Mr. Islam has referred to articles 31 and 44 of the Constitution. He further submitted that the initiation and investigation of the respective criminal case challenged in the writ petitions are the glaring examples of the abuse of the process of Court, so the appellants rightly approached the High Court Division for their protection from such abuse by filing the respective writ petition. Mr Islam further submitted that the High Court Division failed to consider that if the accused take recourse to file an application under section 561A of the Code, then a particular case shall be focused, but in deciding an application under article 102 of the Constitution whole gamut of the fundamental right of the writ-petitioners as guaranteed in the Constitution to be treated in accordance with law shall come into play and exercise of such power by the High Court Division is also necessary to ensure its superintendence and control over the Sub-ordinate Courts and Tribunals as mandated in article 109 of the Constitution and thus, erred in law in holding that the writ petitions were not maintainable.

96. In respect of Civil Appeal No. 12 of 2011 Mr Islam submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court Division having correctly found that the writ petition was maintainable erred in law in not setting-aside/quashing proceedings as contained in CR Case No. 3518 dated 9-10-2007 pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka inasmuch as the allegations made in the petition of complaint filed by the Registrar do not at all attract the mischief of section 397 of the Act, 1994.

97. In conclusion Mr Islam submitted that all appeals be allowed and the leave petition be disposed of by quashing the respective criminal proceeding challenged in the respective writ petition.

98. Ms OK Kyung Oh, respondent No. 3 in the appeals as well as respondent No. 6 in the leave petition appearing in person submitted that the respective criminal case sought to be quashed/set-aside by filing the respective writ petition is independent of each other as well as other cases filed by her having altogether different allegations which, therefore, cannot be termed to be harassing and malafide. She further submitted that the cases involved in Civil Appeal Nos.  11 and 13 of 2011 being at the stage of investigation and the investigating authority being authorized by law to carry on with such investigation, the same cannot be quashed / set-aside. She further submitted that in the case involved in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1159 of 2011 the police after investigation having found prima-facie case already submit-ted charge-sheet against the accused, the question of quashing/setting-aside the same by the High Court Division in exercising jurisdiction under article 102 of the Constitution does not arise at all. She further submitted that the accused having committed an offence within the meaning of section 397 of the Act, 1994 by filing the false annual report and the forged resignation letter allegedly signed by her, the Registrar rightly filed the petition of complaint before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka who having found prima-facie case rightly took cognizance in the case, the truth of which shall be decided on the basis of evidence to be adduced during the trial. She lastly submitted that the writ petitions were not maintainable as the writ-petitioners had other alternative forum under the Code if they at all felt aggrieved because of the respective impugned case and further the allegations of the commission of offence by the accused made in the respective case being question of fact cannot be decided in writ jurisdiction and, as such, all appeals and the leave petition are liable to be dismissed.

99. From the judgments of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition Nos. 7610 of 2008 and 10171 of 2007, it appears that the learned Judges considering the principle of law enunciated in the cases of Dhaka Ware House Limited vs Assistant Collector reported in 11 BLD (AD) 227 and Haryana vs Bhajan Lal reported in AIR 1992 (SC) 604 held that the writ petitions were not maintainable as the petitioners had equally efficacious remedy under the Code for redress of their grievances. Besides deciding the question of maintainability, the learned Judges also considered the merit of the respective cases and observed that the allegations of creation of some forged and false notices and resolutions of the Board meeting of the Company as made in the petition of complaint giving rise to Joydebpur Police Station Case No.  53 dated 14-8-2008 corresponding to GR Case No. 915 of 2008 being very much clear and specific, there was no scope of telling that the allegations complained of in the case was inextricably mixed up; the police having started investigation of the case as per order of the Magistrate it could not be said that the offence complained of being non-cognizable the investigation of the same by the police without order of the Magistrate was without jurisdiction, so could be challenged in writ jurisdiction; before completion of investigation it cannot be said at all that the case is malafide or it has been instituted maliciously; there is no reason at all for stopping investigation of the case in question at this stage; after completion of investigation and submission of the police report the Court concerned will decide whether this case can be proceeded further or not and the accused writ-petitioners will also have then opportunity to plead their case before that Court at proper stage. The learned Judges considering sections 463 and 464 of the Penal Code while dealing with the merit of GR Case No.  922 of 2007 challenged in Writ Petition No.  10171 of 2007 observed that there was clear allegation of making false document in the FIR giving rise to the said GR Case. The argument made by the learned Advocate for the writ petitioners that the allegations made in the FIR, even if, taken to be true then also it cannot be termed "making a false document" as there is no element of dishonesty or fraud as mentioned in section 464 of the Penal Code and that the petitioners had no intention to cause damage or injury to the informant cannot be accepted at this initial stage of investigation. The learned Judges further observed that in the circumstances it could not be said that there was no ingredient of forgery in the allegation made in the case.

100. In both judgments, the learned Judges further observed that the allegations made in the two cases (one having arisen out of a petition of complaint and the other out of an FIR) challenged in two writ petitions and the other cases filed by respondent No. 3 were not same and similar as argued by the learned Counsel for the appellants. In both cases, the learned Judges concluded by saying that in the facts and circumstances of the case, there was no reason for stopping the further proceedings of the respective criminal case at the stage of investigation.

101. From the judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2007 giving rise to Civil Appeal No. 12 of 2011, it appears that the learned Judges found the writ petition maintainable though they observed that—

"Authorities stemming from the superior Courts from our as well as from other common law jurisdictions, surmon that as general rule judicial review proceedings cannot be resorted" to where statutes provide Builtin dispute resolution mechanism"

102. In finding the writ petition maintain-able, the learned Judges further observed that devices provided by section 561A of the Code were not appropriate in challenging the Registrar's decision or action of filing the complaint case. Then the learned Judges came to the finding that—

"Moreover, this is a case where interpretation, not only of Sections 397 and 393, But also of many other sections of the Act, are to be explored in order to find out whether or not the alleged forged letter belongs to the group of documents that are required by or for the purpose of any of the provisions of this act. So, according to the ratio decidendi expressed in the cases reported in 40 DLR (AD) 206 and 60 DLR (AD) 147, Supra, this is also a case which deserves departure from the cardinal principle that judicial review cannot be resorted to where statutory remedies are entailed".

103. After finding the writ petition maintainable, the learned Judges dealt with the merit of the case and considering section 397 of the Act, 1994 held that it was abundantly clear that a person could be indicted under section 397 of the Act only in a situation, where, through any document, required by or for the purpose of any of the provisions of this Act, willfully made statement which was false in any material particular and it was a sine quo non to initiate a proceeding under section 397 of the Act, 1994 that the document concerned was of a kind that "is required by or for the purpose of any provision of the Act" and finally concluded that the complaint filed by the Registrar giving rise to the case in question was maintainable in law but the alleged resignation letter as complained of in the petition of complaint did not belong to the—

"herd of documents, Section 397 envisages the Registrar's action in including the said allegedly forged resignation letter in the complaint petition, went far beyond what section 397 contemplates. A fortiori, the Court below also cannot take the said alleged resignation letter into consideration,";

the allegation in respect of the 'annual return on the capital' of the Company, was also referred to in the complaint petition, albeit with apparently lesser emphasis belonged to the class of documents as envisaged in section 397 of the Act and it would remain open to the Court below to ascertain through examination of witnesses and evidence whether the allegation of false statement in the annual return of the company's capital petition is proved or not.

104. With the above observations and findings the learned Judges discharged the Rule in the following terms:

"In consequence, the proceeding of Complaint Case No. 3518 dated 9-10-2007, initiated by the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies and Firms, now pending in the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, under section 397 of the Companies Act, 1994, will continue, but the alleged resignation letter, as mentioned in the complaint petition by the Registrar, shall not be taken into account by the Court below in considering whether an offence under section 397 of the Act has been proved or not."

105. In view of the findings given by 3(three) separate Benches, in 4(four) writ petitions as summarized hereinbefore, the points on which leave has been granted, the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the appellants and the leave petitioners and Ms Ok-Kyung Oh, (respondent No. 3 in the appeals and respondent No. 6 in the leave petition) who appeared in person the core question to be decided by us is whether the respective writ petition, filed before the High Court Division was maintainable in law though the writ-petitioners had other alternative remedy under the Code to redress their grievances. Before we enter into the discussion of the question, we are constrained to observe that the learned Judges of the High Court Division adopted an apparent wrong procedure in passing the judgment and order in Writ Petition Nos. 7610 of 2008 and 10171 of 2007, in that in both writ petitions they first examined the merit of the contentions raised by the learned Advocate for the writ petitioners as to the merit of the respective case challenged in the respective writ petition and then decided the question of maintainability. When the question of maintainability of a writ petition is raised by the contesting respondents, it is the first and foremost duty of the learned Judges to decide the said question first. If the writ petitions are not found maintainable, then it will be sheer wastage of Court's valuable time to consider and discuss the merit of the case. In the affidavit-in-oppositions filed by the contesting respondents in Writ Petition Nos. 7610 of 2008 and 10171 of 2007, it having been specifically contended that the writ petitions were not maintainable as the petitioners had an alternative equally efficacious remedy under section 561A of the Code, it was incumbent upon the learned Judges to decide the said question first and if they found the writ petition maintainable and then only could embark upon the merit of the respective case.

106. In deciding the question whether the respective writ petition was maintainable or not, we are to see the back ground of the respective criminal case, the proceedings of which were challenged therein even at the risk of repetition, because the power of judicial review to be exercised by the High Court Division under article 102 of the Constitution is a discretionary one and before exercising such power the High Court Division has to be satisfied whether in the facts and circumstances of a particular case and the law relating thereto interference by way judicial review is at all called for or necessary.

107. In Writ Petition No. 7610 of 2008 giving rise to Civil Appeal No.  11 of 2011, the petitioners prayed for issuance of a Rule calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why all further proceedings/investigation of GR Case No. 915 of 2008 corresponding to Joydebpur Police Station Case No. 53 dated 14-8-2008 pending in the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gazipur "Being malice in fact and malice in law" should not be set-aside in order to prevent abuse of the process of Court and in order to secure ends of justice though Rule was issued in a modified form as has been stated at the beginning of the judgment. This case has arisen out of a petition of complaint filed by respondent No. 3 before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gazipur. The complaint petition having been filed before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gazipur, he sent the same to the Officer-in-Charge of Joydebpur police station for investigation and for taking action in accordance with law. The Officer-in-Charge of the police station having treated the petition of complaint as FIR started the case under sections 406/420/468/47 of the Penal Code and the case is under investigation. The main allegation made in the petition of complaint is that the accused in collusion with each other fabricated a number of Board meeting notices and resolutions in order to oust the complainant from the post of Managing Director of the Company.

108. In Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2007 giving rise to Civil Appeal No.  12 of 2011, prayer was made for issuing a Rule calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why all further proceedings of CR Case No. 3518 dated 9-10-2007 pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka initiated by the Registrar "without any lawful authority being outside the perimeters of section 397 of the Companies Act, 1994" should not be quashed/set-aside as being malafide and illegal and is of no legal effect in order to prevent abuse of the process of Court and in order to secure the ends of justice although Rule was issued in a modified form. In this case the complainant is the Registrar. The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka took cognizance in the case on 9-10-2007 against the accused under section 397 of the Act, 1994. The allegations made in the petition of complaint are that the resignation letter of respondent No. 3 kept in the office of the Registrar was forged which was created by the accused in collusion with each other. Accused Abul Bashar, the income tax consultant submitted Forms 23 B, balance sheet and the disputed resignation letter along with some other documents and the signature of respondent No. 3 was forged to file those documents.

109. In Writ Petition No.  10171 of 2007 giving rise to Civil Appeal No.  13 of 2011 prayer was made to issue a Rule Nisi calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why all further proceedings of GR Case No. 922 of 2007 corresponding to Joydebpur Police Station Case No. 83(9)02 dated 30-9-2007 pending in the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gazipur being "malice in fact and malice in law" should not be set-side in order to prevent abuse of the process of Court and in order to secure ends of justice though Rule was issued in a modified form. This case arose on the basis of an FIR lodged by respondent No. 3 with Joydebpur Police Station on 30-9-2007 alleging that on 30th June, summary of share capital was submitted in the office of the Registrar under her signature, though she was in Korea at that time, therefore, her signature in the documents submitted before the Registrar was forged. Accused No. 3 Mr Zahid Karim Chowdhury submitted all documents to the government authority. Mr Zahid Karim Chowdhury in collusion with accused No. 2, Bo Sun Park and Han Sik Kim forged her signature and accordingly, prayed for initiation of the case against the accused under the appropriate provision of law for committing the offence of forgery. The case is under investigation.

110. The proceedings of the case challenged in Writ Petition No.  10675 of 2008 giving rise to Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1159 of 2011 is GR Case No. 746 of 2007 arising out of Motijheel Police Station Case No. 86 dated 19-7-2007. This case was started on the basis of an FIR lodged by respondent No. 6 with the said police station alleging the commission of an offence under sections 385/109/506 of the Penal Code against leave petitioner No. 2, Mr Bo Sun Park and 3(three) others (leave petitioner No. 1 is the Company). In this case after investigation, police submitted charge-sheet on 4-12-2007 under sections 468/201/385/506/109 of the Penal Code against leave petitioner No. 2 and 2(two) others.

111. From a consideration of the petition of complaint and the FIR's giving rise to the respective criminal proceeding challenged in the respective writ petition in a circuitous way it is clear that out of 4(four) cases, 3(three) were filed by respondent No. 3 of Civil Appeal Nos. 11 and 13 of 2011 as well as respondent No. 6 of Civil Petition for Leave Appeal No. 1159 of 2011. Again of these 3(three) cases after completion of investigation charge-sheet has already been submitted in the case involved in the leave petition. Of the two other cases, GR Case No. 915 of 2008 has arisen out of a petition of complaint filed before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gazipur and GR Case No. 922 of 2007 has arisen out of an FIR. The remaining case being CR No.  3518 of 2007 has arisen out of a petition of complaint filed by the Registrar under section 397 of the Act, 1994. Mr Amir-ul-Islam could not show any lack of jurisdiction on the part of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gazipur in entertaining the petition of complaint filed by the complainant (respondent No. 3) and then sending the same to the Officer-in-Charge, Joydebpur police station to investigate and to take other legal action and then treating the same as FIR and starting the police station case in question by the said police station giving rise to GR Case No. 915 of 2008 challenged in Writ Petition No. 7610 of 2008, so also in entertaining the petition of complaint by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka filed by the Registrar and taking cognizance in the case against the accused under section 397 of the Act, 1994 giving rise to CR Case No. 3518 of 2007 challenged in Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2007. Mr. Amir-ul-Islam could not also show any procedural defect in recording the FIR by the police of Joydebpur police station lodged by respondent No.  3 giving rise Joydebpur police station Case No.  83(9)07 corresponding to GR Case No. 922 of 2007 challenged in Writ Petition No.  10171 of 2007.

112. Although the learned Judge found Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2007 maintainable on the view that

"Devices provided 6y section 561A, in our view, is not appropriate in challenging the Registrar's decision or action of finding the complaint case. Moreover, this is a case where interpretation, not only of Sections 397 and 393, but also of many other Sections of the Act, are to be explored in order to find' out whether or not the alleged forged letter belongs to the group of documents that are required by or for the purpose of any of the provisions of this Act,"

from a plain reading of the petition of complaint, it appears to us that no interpretation either of section 397 or 393 of the Act, 1994 or any other section of the said Act is involved. This will be clearer if the petition of complaint is gone into which is as follows :—

৪। Ms Ok Kyung Oh  এ পরিদপ্তরে ৪-১-২০০৫ তারিখে একটি অভিযোগ পত্র দাখিল করতঃ জানান যে, তিনি পরিচালক এবং ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক পদ হতে পদত্যাগ করেননি এবং এ পরিদ্প্তরের রেকর্ড রক্ষিত পদত্যাগ পত্রটিতে তাহার স্বাক্ষর জাল করা হয়েছে। এ বিষয়ে তিনি বানিজ্য মন্ত্রনালয়, বিনিয়োগ (sic) বোর্ডসহ সকল কর্তৃপক্ষকে অনুলিপির মাধ্যমে অবগত করেন।

৫। গত ৩-১-২০০৭ইং তারিখে ট্যাক্স ফোর্স-২এর কমান্ডার এবং তার সহযোগী কর্মকর্তাবৃন্দসহ Ms Ok Kyung Oh সহকারে এ পরিদপ্তরে আসেন এবং নিবন্ধক মহোদয়ের কক্ষে বসে  Ms Ok Kyung Oh এর ১-১-২০০৫ইং তারিখে (৪-১-২০০৫ইং তারিখে দাখিলকৃত) অভিযোগপত্র বিষয় সংশ্লিষ্ট নথিপত্র পরীক্ষা করা হয়। তর্কিত পদত্যাগ পত্রটি পরীক্ষা নিরীক্ষা করে দেখা যায় পদত্যাগ পত্রে প্রদত্ত  Ms Ok Kyung Oh এর স্বাক্ষর কোম্পানীর সংঘ স্মারক ও সংঘবিধির স্বাক্ষেরের সাথে গড়মিল রয়েছে।

৬। নথিতে দেখা যায় যে, আয়কর আইনজীবী জনাব আবুল বাশার, ২৫, ইন্দ্ররা রোড, ঢাকা Mr Bo Sun Park  কর্তৃক ২৭-৭-২০০৫ তারিখে এ পরিদপ্তরে কাগজপত্র সংশোধন ও দাখিলের বিষয কোম্পানীর প্রতিনিধি নিযুক্ত হয়েছেন বলে জানান। জনাব আবুল বাশার ১-৮-২০০৫ তারিখে কোম্পানীর পক্ষে বার্ষিক মূলধনের বিবরণী, ফরম ২৩/বি, ব্যালেন্সশীট দাখিল করেন। বিবরনীতে

Ms Ok Kyung Oh  অভিযোগকারীকে ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক হিসাবে দেখানো হয়নি। তাছাড়া তর্কিত পদত্যাগ পত্রটিও জনাব আবুল বাশার (৩নং আসামী) এ পরিদপ্তরের দাখিল করেন। ৩নং আসামী মিথ্যা বিবৃতি সম্বলিত অর্থাৎ জাল পদত্যাগ পত্রের সুবাদে  Ms Ok Kyung Oh  পরিচালক ও ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক পদ থেকে অপসারিত দেখিয়ে বাদী বরাবরে ১ আসামী Mr. Bo sun Park স্বাক্ষরিত পরিচালকের তালিকা দাখিল করেন।

৭। বাদী দপ্তরে রক্ষিত খাতগুলি পর্যালোচনা করে প্রতীয়মান হয়েছে যে, আসামীগন পরস্পর যোগসাজসে Ms Ok Kyung এর স্বাক্ষর জাল করে তর্কিত তারিখ বিহীন পদত্যাগ পত্র সৃজন করেছেন এবং উহার সুবাদে মিথ্যা বিবৃতি প্রদান করে ৯-২-২০০৪ ও ৭-২-২০০৫ তারিখে পরিচালকের তালিকাটি নথিভুক্ত করেছেন। আসামীগনের যোগসাজশীমূলক তৎপরতা এবং মিথ্যা বিবৃতির বিষয়টি দিবালোকের মত স্পষ্ট। তাদের দাখিলকৃত ৯-২-২০০৪ তারিখের পরিচালকের তালিকা Ms Ok Kyung Oh কে পরিচালক ও ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক পদে নতুন করে নিযুক্ত দেখানো হয়েছে। অতঃপর ২৮-৫-২০০৫ তারিখে পরিচালক ও ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক পদে নতুন নিযুক্ত দেখানো হয়েছে। সর্বশেষ ৭-৫-২০০৫ তারিখে Ms Ok Kyung Oh কে পরিচালক ও ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক পদ থেকে অপসারন দেখানো হয়েছে। এতে পরিস্কার বুঝা যায় যে, ৯-২-২০০৪, ২৮-৫-২০০৫ ও ৭-২-২০০৫ তারিখে পরিচালক তালিকাগুলি আসামীগন কর্তৃক যোগসাজশীমূলক ভাবে মিথ্যা বিবৃতির মাধ্যমে সৃজিত।

৮। Ms Ok Kyung বাদী বরাবরে আরো একটি অভিযোগপত্র দাখিল করেন এবং ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক পক্ষে পুনঃ বহালের আবেদন করেন এবং একই সাথে জানান যে, ৩০-৬-২০০৪, তারিখে সমাপ্ত বছরের বার্ষিক মূলধনের বিবরণী তার জাল স্বাক্ষরের বাদীর দপ্তরে দাখিল করা হয়েছে। উক্ত স্বাক্ষরটিও জাল  Ms Ok Kyung Oh  বিবরনীতে স্বাক্ষর দেননি, বরং তিনি ঐ সময় কোরিযায় ছিলেন। উক্ত বিবরনীতে কোম্পানীর শেয়ার ও পরিচালকের অবস্থা সঠিকভাবে প্রতিফলিত হয়নি।

উপরোক্ত অবস্থাধনে কোম্পানী আইন, ১৯৯৪ এর ৩৯৭ ধারা মতে কোম্পানীর ৯-২-২০০৪, ২৮-৫-২০০৫ ও ৭-২-২০০৫ তারিখে পরিচালকের তালিকা এবং ৩০-৬-২০০৪ তারিখের বার্ষিক মূলধনের বিবরনীতে মিথ্যা বিবৃতি প্রদান করায় আসামীগনের বিরুদ্ধে শাস্তিমূলক ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করিতে মর্জি হয়।

সংযুক্তঃ জাল স্বাক্ষর সম্বলিত কথিত পদত্যাগপত্র, পরিচালকের তালিকা এবং সংঘ স্বারক ও বিধির স্বাক্ষরসমূহের ছায়ালিপি।

113. On going through the provisions of sections 397 and 393 of the Act, 1994, we do not see any ambiguity in the languages used in the said two sections vis-a-vis the allegations made in the petition of complaint warranting any interpretation thereof or any other section of the Act, 1994 "or any exploration" as to whether the alleged forged resignation letter mentioned in the petition of complaint belongs to the group of the documents mentioned in the said two sections as observed by the learned Judges to make the writ petition amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division. It is also to be noted that although with the observations as quoted above the learned Judges found the writ petition maintainable, the discussions made in the judgment about section 397 of the Act, 1994 does not show any such reflection. In this regard it is pertinent to state that the learned Judges clearly observed that the proceedings of the CR Case in question initiated by the Registrar "will continue", that means there was no lack of jurisdiction on the part of the Chief Judicial Magistrate in taking cognizance in the case against the accused and then in proceeding with the same, if that be so, how could the learned Judges observe that

"but the alleged resignation letter, as mentioned in the complaint petition by the Registrar shall not be taken into account by the Court below in considering 397 of the Act has been proved or not."

114. Whether the resignation letter of respondent No. 3 shall be treated as a document within the meaning of section 397 of the Act, 1994 is the domain of the trial Court and before holding the trial, there is no scope of dissecting the allegations made in the petition of complaint as has been done by the learned Judges and in doing so they exceeded their jurisdiction.

<u>115. So far as the criminal proceedings challenged in the leave petition is concerned after investigation the police having already submit-ted charge-sheet against leave petitioner No. 2 and 2(two) others, we do not see any scope of challenging the same by invoking the power of judicial review of the High Court Division, as submission of charge-sheet shows prima-facie truth in the allegations made in the FIR and that definitely involves facts which cannot be resolved in a summary proceeding like writ petition). However, still leave petitioner No. 2 can invoke the alternative forum under section 561A of the Code as has been observed by the High Court Division in the impugned judgment.</u>

<u>116. In the writ petitions not a single ground was taken with reference to the fundamental rights as guaranteed in the Constitution to a citizen and every other person. The grounds were taken only to the effect that the respective criminal case was harassing and nudafide and from the prayer of the respective writ petition as quoted hereinbefore it is apparent that the writ-petitioners sought to quash/set-aside the respective impugned proceeding as "malice in fact and malice in law" and to prevent abuse of the process of Court as well as to secure the ends of justice. The prayers in the writ petitions were not couched in the language as articulated in article 102 of the Constitution. Reading the grounds and the prayers made in the respective writ petition, it appears that in fact the petitioners came before the High Court Division to set-aside/quash the proceedings invoking its inherent power under section 561A of the Code, but wrongly styled the application under article 102 of the Constitution. That being the state of the writ petitions those did not at all deserve any consideration by way of interference by the High Court Division issuing Rule in exercising its power of judicial review. Before issuance of the Rule the learned Judges had a responsibility to see as to whether the cause title and the prayer of the writ petition conformed with the language of article 102 of the Constitution and the High Court Division Rules and whether the facts and circumstances of the case at all warranted any interference by way of judicial review. But unfortunately, as it appears the learned Judges were totally oblivious about the above responsibility and issued the Rule as a routine work. This kind of exercise of power by the High Court Division is disapproved by this Division.</u>

117. Before this Division, Mr Islam has referred to articles 31 and 44 of the Constitution to substantiate his argument that the High Court Division in exercise of its power of judicial review can quash/set-aside a criminal proceeding to prevent abuse of the process of law as well as the process of the sub-ordinate Court in order to save a citizen or any other person from being harassed in a malaftde manner from the point of constitutional concept of protecting a citizen and any other person from being harassed unnecessarily. We do not find any rationality behind this submission of Mr Islam inasmuch as, he has not been able to show violation of any law or point out any procedural mistake committed by the concerned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate in taking cognizance in the case against the accused in CR Case No. 3518 of 2007 and in starting the respective police case by the police challenged in the respective writ petition and then in investigating the same and thus to show any abuse of the law and the process of Court to avail the power of judicial review of the High Court Division under article 102 of the Constitution to protect the fundamental right of the accused as guaranteed in article 31 of the Constitution or any other fundamental right. In the facts and circumstances of the respective criminal case, we find nothing to apply the principle of constitutional concept of protecting the accused from being harassed as argued by Mr Islam. It is to be noted that in all the cases the accused-petitioners surrendered before the concerned Magistrate and they were enlarged on bail. So, the fundamental right of the accused as guar-anteed in article 31 of the Constitution to the protection of law, and to be treated in accordance with law and only in accordance with law has in no way been infringed.

<u>118. We find no force in the argument of Mr Amir-ul-Islam that the High Court Division could very much protect the accused from harassment because of the filing of series of cases by respondent No. 3 as well as respondent No. 6 centering the fact of her alleged forged resignation letter submitted in the office of the Registrar by quashing/setting-aside the impugned criminal proceedings inasmuch as, the locus standi or authority of a private person in lodging an FIR and in filing a petition of complaint in her private capacity about the commission of an offence in relation to her body or property cannot be stopped by the High Court Division in exercising the power of judicial review under article 102 of the Constitution and such scheme has not been conceived of in the Constitution. In this context we like to observe that in the writ petitions neither the jurisdiction of the Magistrates where the cases are pending nor the authority of the investigation officer to investigate the impugned cases has been challenged and in none of the cases question of law as well as interpretation of any statute is involved. Mr Islam has also failed to show with reference to any law that the concerned Magistrates where the cases are pending and the investigating authorities investigating the respective cases have/had no jurisdiction to proceed with the cases and to investigate the allegations made in the respective FIR. In all 4(four) writ petitions catchy legal phraseology such as 'malice in fact' and 'malice in law' have been used without feeding back how the cases can be termed to be 'malice in law and 'malice in fact'. When a private individual is authorized by law to bring allegations about the commission of an offence by a person and there is no dearth of jurisdiction of the Court in dealing with such cases as well as the police to investigate the allegations then how those proceedings can be termed to be 'malice in law' and 'malice in fact' and declared to have been taken or made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. However, if the accused feel that they are being harassed in a malafide manner through the filing of series of cases over the selfsame incident or allegation they have other forum to redress such harassment but not the special original jurisdiction of the High Court Division.</u>

119. We equally do not find any substance in the submission of Mr Amir-ul-Islam that if the accused take recourse to the alternative remedy by way of filing application under section 561A of the Code then a particular case will be focused whereas in an application under article 102 of the Constitution the fundamental rights as guaranteed to them shall come into play inasmuch as from the prayer made in each of the writ petitions as have been quoted hereinbefore it is apparent that a particular criminal proceeding was challenged therein and the whole intention of the accused behind filing the respective writ petition was to quash/set-aside the respective proceeding challenged therein and the Rule was also issued in modified form only about the particular proceeding.

<u>120. We also failed to see any logic behind the argument of Mr Amir-ul-Islam that in order to exercise the power of superintendence and control over the Sub-ordinate Courts and Tribunals as mandated in article 109 of the Constitution, the High Court Division can really exercise its power of judicial review and thus, interfere with the proceedings of the Sub-ordinate Courts and Tribunals. It is expected that the impugned proceedings challenged in the writ petitions having arisen out of the petition of complaint and the FIR by an individual as well as by a designated Government official shall be dealt with by the concerned Magistrate/Court in accordance with the provisions as laid down in the Code. In case the concerned Magistrate/Court does not deal with the cases in accordance with law as provided in the Code or the accused are not treated in accordance with law, they shall have every right to take recourse to the provisions of the Code inclusive of section 561A there of as observed in the impugned judgments. So, the question of superintendence and control by the High Court Division under article 109 of the Constitution over the Magistrates where the impugned proceedings/cases are pending by way of interference through judicial review does not arise at all. The submission of Mr Islam in this respect appears to us misconceived.</u>

121. Mr Amir-ul-Islam, in support of his contention that, in spite of the availability of the statutory alternative forum under the Code, the High Court Division could really exercise its power of judicial review and quash/set-aside the impugned proceedings challenged in the respective writ petition, tried to rely upon the cases of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd vs Assistant Collector of Customs reported in 11 BLD (AD) 227, Nesar Ahmed also known as Babul vs Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commission, Noakhali reported in 49 DLR (AD) 111, the Government of the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh vs lqbal Hasan Mahmood alias Iqbal Hasan Mahmood Tuku reported in 60 DLR (AD) 147 and State of Haryana vs Ch. Bhajan Lal reported in AIR 1992 (SC) 604. But in the context of the respective criminal proceeding challenged in the respective writ petition as discussed above, the principles of law enunciated in the said reported cases have got no manner of application and those do not at all help Mr Islam to substantiate his argument that the respective writ petition was maintainable and we do not consider it at all necessary to discuss the facts and circumstances of those cases in detail under which the principles of law were enunciated in those cases.

122. In conclusion, we hold that the writ petitions giving rise to the appeals and the leave petition were not maintainable. As we have already held that the writ petitions were not maintainable, the observations made by the High Court Division in the impugned judgments touching the merit of the respective case cannot stand and accordingly those are expunged.

123. Since we have found the writ petitions not maintainable, we consider it indiscreet to dwell upon the incidental points on which leave was also granted. If we do so, that may prejudice either party in case the writ-petitioners choose to seek remedy in the alternative forum under the Code.

124. For the reasons stated hereinbefore, the appeals and the leave petition are dismissed without any order as to cost.

Md Mamtaz Uddin Ahmed J: I have gone through the separate judgments prepared by my learned brother, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J and my learned brother, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J. I agree with the judgment of my learned brother, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J.

Md Shamsul Huda J: I have gone through the separate judgments prepared by my learned brother, Surendra Kumar Sinha J and my learned brother, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J. I agree with the judgment of my learned brother, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J.

full_judgment:
Kashefa Hussain J : This is an application by the Defendant-Appellant-Petitioners for review of judgment and decree dated 5-12-2010 passed by this Division in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998. Upon filing of the instant Review Application, Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 5-12-2010 passed in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 by the High Court Division should not be reviewed and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The facts of the case in a nutshell, are that the appellants filed First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 before the High Court Division being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 9-10-1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 79 of 194 decreeing the suit. In the First Appeal, the appellant's contention inter alia was that the Respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 79 of 1994 before the aforesaid Court seeking partition of the land and that it belonged to one Hossain Sheikh. The plaintiff stated inter alia, that Hossain Sheikh died leaving behind one son Akam Uddin and a daughter Samela Bibi who was plaintiff in the suit. Samela Bibi as per the plaint inherited 1/3 rd share to the land under partition and the rest 2/3rd was inherited by Akam Uddin and Akam Uddin died leaving behind 2 sons Abdul Hakim Sheikh and Abu Zafor Sheikh one wife Chutu Bibi and a daughter Romesa Khatun. Akam Uddin created a registered deed of patta dated 29-11-1927 showing settlement of 5.27 acres of land in his favour measuring 14 annas share in the property of Hossain Sheikh and 2 annas were left out of settlement. 

3. It is the plaintiffs case that the patta was a unilateral patta and was not registered by both the parties and since both Samela Bibi and her brother Akam Uddin were both minors at the time such patta was void. The plaintiff further stated that there were several previous litigations and the patta deed was cancelled. But the plaintiffs names in the suit property was not recorded as per her 1/3 rd share and this compelled her to file the partition suit claiming 1/3rd share of the suit land. 

4. The defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint, contending inter alia, that Hosain Sheikh had lawfully settled the suit land in favour of Akam Uddin by a registered patta deed dated 29-11-1927 and that after the settlement there remaining only 2 annas share to be divided between the heirs accordingly to their proportionate shares, Akam Uddin started possessing 4.60 acres of land and died leaving behind 2 sons and his legal heirs inherited the suit land proportionately and in this manner the defendant No.2 inherited 1/5 th share in the suit land. Abdul Hakim being in possession transferred 1.54 acres of land by registered kabalas deed dated 4-4-1984 in favour of defendant No. 1. During possession the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 also purchased lands by a number of kabala deeds and the defendant No. 1 disclosed that they are in possession of the entire land except 20 decimals of such land. 

5. During trial six issues were framed, the PWs and PWs were duly examined and exhibits were duly produced before the Court and after conclusion of the trial the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Khulna decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 9-10-1997 ascertaining the share of the plaintiff to the extent of 1.60 acres and ascertaining the share of Akam Uddin to the extent of 2/3rd shares. 6. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree dated 9-4-1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 79 of 1994, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 preferred First Appeal being No. 177 of 1998 before this division and alter hearing both sides and upon scrutiny of materials on record, this division allowed the appeal mainly on the ground of defect Of parties and the requirement of the suit land to be brought into the hotchpotch of the suit. Although the appeal was allowed yet the appellants preferred this review application before us arising out of First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 on a specific ground of law. The petitioners in the review petition stated that due to unavoidable circumstances beyond their control they could not file an appeal against the judgment passed by the High Court Division and by the time they were ready to file an appeal, time for filing an appeal before the Appellate Division had already expired. They also stated in their review petition that the plaintiff-respondent in First Appeal 'No. 177 of 1998 after dismissal of their suit filed a new suit afresh in the Court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna and summons of such suit was received and only after obtaining the certified copy, of the judgment the engaged Advocate from the Khulna Bar for the first time pointed out that there was an adverse finding on law points in the judgment of the High Court Division. But due to circumstances beyond their control there was no time to file an appeal before the High Court Division and due to such unavoidable circumstances the review application was also filed with a delay of 445 days and such delay was wholly unintentional. 

7. Mr Abul Kalam Mainuddin with Mr M Shamsul Haque, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the review petitioners while Mr M Qumrul Haque Siddique with Mr Tushar Kanti Roy, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the respondent-opposite-parties to resist the Rule. 

8. Mr Abul Kalam Mainuddin, the learned Advocate for the review petitioner while making his submissions mainly cast his thrust upon the issue of amendment of section 107 of the Transfer Property Act particularly the date of the amendment. He takes us through the judgment passed in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 and points out that this Division in its judgment made an error in law in not taking into consideration the fact that the patta deed in question was executed on 29-11-1927 which was before the subsequent amendment of section 107, which amendment came in 1929 only after the execution of the deed on 29-11-1927. He agitated before us that therefore the amended version of section 107 requiring a patta deed to be executed by both the parties was not required before 1929 and consequently in the instant case shall not to be applicable to the patta deed dated 29-11-1927. He also argues before us that he had agitated the issue of amendment of 1929 and the date of the execution of the patta deed before this Division while making his submissions during the hearing in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 and further asserts that their submissions were also noted down in the judgment, but that this Division upon an error of law missed out on the legal bar of specific point not being able to give retrospective effect to a new provision of statute under the law. He further attracts our attention to a finding by this Division in its judgment that the land is agricultural land. The learned Advocate strenuously argued that in spite of express sub-missions made by them on the issue of the amendment of 1929 and the non-applicability of such amendment relating to a deed executed at a prior date, yet the submissions of the appellant-petitioner remained unanswered, not addressed upon by the Court. He also persuades that having obtained knowledge of the adverse remark much later due to circumstances beyond their control, the petitioners finding no other alternative was compelled to file a review application praying before this Division for review of its own judgments. 

9. Upon queries made by us as to the legality of filing a review application on the grounds taken by the parties, the learned Advocate for the review petitioners submits that a review application is allowable in this case since this Division in his judgment made an error apparent on the face of the record and therefore according to the learned Advocate. Review will lie in the instant case. Upon further queries the learned Advocate agitated before us that there is an error apparent on the face of the record in the judgment of this Division since this Division by not addressing itself upon an important of law rather remained 'silent' on the point and thus made a 'mistake' and due to which review petition lies. 

10. On the other hand, Mr M Quamrul Haque Siddique, the learned Advocate for the respondent-opposite parties submits that this Division cannot sit on its own judgment save for few limited purposes. He points out that no new point of law was agitated and stresses upon the point that in a case where the issue was agitated before the Court but which not addressed by it, in such cases review shall not lie. He reiterated the point that this Division cannot review its own judgment on an issue which was already before it and such issue was expressly agitated before it but it was not addressed for some reason. He points out that in this event of an issue being raised even if it is then only it upon a specific point of law can be only subject of an appeal. 

11. We have heard the learned Advocates from both sides, perused the application for review, judgments and materials on records. It transpires from the judgment passed in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 by this Division that it is true that the review petitioners had placed their submissions upon a specific point of law, but the Court had not addressed on that point. 

12. The situation might have been different if the particular issue was not placed before the Court at all. But since in the judgment itself, their Lordships even noted the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the appellant-review-petitioners we do not have any scope to presume that the Court might inadvertently upon an error mistakenly or consciously overlooked the issue. It is obvious from the records that the issue was placed before the Court, but their Lordships decided not to address itself upon the same or did not feel it necessary to address the point same and now in remained passive and apathetic. Now, in a situation like this whether review petition shall lie against the Court's conscious passiveness and apathy or whether it is a subject of appeal, we must at first examine the provisions of a review application within the scope of order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads under. 

13. Upon a perusal of Order 47 and an analysis of the circumstances under which a review of a judgment may lie, as is quite obvious from the judgment itself, that no new and important matter of evidence was discovered in this case after the passing of the judgment and decree. As we discussed above, it was upon a specific point of law and such point was already submitted by the concerned counsels, as appears from the judgment itself. Hence, it does not prima-facie come within the ambit of any new and hereto before undiscovered or unraveled and important matter of evidence. 

14. Another circumstance as provided for in Order 47 for a review to be maintainable is "on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record". Here also we feel it necessary to reiterate that in this case it was not an inadvertent "mistake" or "error" by which the Court might have overlooked a specific issue. It if was, in fact an inadvertent mistake or error, review would lie. But as is obvious, the Court knowingly upon its conscious decision decided not to address the issue, whatever its reason of doing so. Under such circumstances we cannot treat a conscious decision of the Court to be 'mistake' or 'error' apparent on the face of the record. Therefore if any person feels himself aggrieved by such decision taken consciously by a Court, not to address itself upon a particular point, in those cases it should be a subject of appeal, and not review. 

15. During course of the argument, the learned Advocates from both sides had cited a few decisions before us in support of their respective arguments and had attracted our attention towards them and from which we are mentioning some. Learned Advocate for the petitioner had cited the principle in the case of Hosne Ara Begum vs Anwara Begum reported in 5 BLC 111 where the principle of maintainability of review in para 11 of the judgment is produced hereunder :-"A review is permissible only when it is seen that there was an error apparent on the face of the record in recording the judgment and order under review." 

16. The petitioner also referred to the case of Rais Ali vs Jabed Ali reported in 19 DLR 511 where the principle cited is as follows:-"What is the face of the record? The judgment which is pronounced by a Court is the face of the record of that Court. It is true that it is not every kind of error which would attract the provisions of Order 47 of the Code. 

But there is no doubt that the judgment itself is the face of the record, whatever else may or may not be the face." 

17. The principle in the case of Mathura Mohan vs Hazara Khatun reported in 48 DLR 190 was also placed before us in the following terms :-

Order XLVII rule I "When there is an omission on the part of a Court to take notice of a provision of law an application for review under Order XLVII rule I CPC is competent." 18. In the case of Hosne Ara Begum vs Anwara Khatun reported in 5 BLC 111 the principle enumerates the circumstances under which a review may be permissible and maintains that to make a review application maintainable there has to be an error apparent on the face the record. But as we have discussed, in this case before us we do not find any error which is apparent of the record, rather it is a conscious decision of the Court by which it decided not to dwell upon a particular point raised by the party. 19. In the case of Rais Ali vs lobed Ali reported in 19 DLR 511, we find an echo of the principle in the case referred to above and therefore our view on it also remains the same. But we would like to draw the attention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner and remind him that in the 19 DLR case, the Court also significantly made an observation, stating that "not every kind of error would attract the pro-visions of Order XLVII, the Code." Relying upon this observation made in the DLR case we may conclude that just because there is an error in the judgment itself, it shall not make it eligible for a review application under Order XLVII, of the Code. 

20. While drawing our attention to the decision in the case of Mathura Mohan vs Hazera Khatun reported in 48 DLR 191, we find that the petitioner had relied upon the principle that in the event of an 'omission' by a Court to take 'notice' of a particular provision of law, Order XLVII, will come into play. But as we analyzed above, in the case before us and as it appears from the judgment in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998, the fact remains that in this particular case, there are no omissions by the Court to take 'notice' of a specific provision of law. In fact as is evident from the judgment itself, the Court did take notice of the particular provision of law by way of including the submissions of the learned Advocate on the particular point in the judgment itself. It is only that the Court unmistakably noted the particular assertion on a point of law, but knowingly decided not to address the issue and left it at that. It is certainly not an omission on the part of the Court, but a decision by the Court having full knowledge. 

21. Therefore we find that the petitioner's reliance upon these judgments are misplaced and he has upon misinterpretation of particular circumstances and the provision of law wrongly relied upon these judgment. 

22. Parallelly, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties relying upon a few judgments, placed those before us for our appreciation some among which we find necessary and significant to examine. The decision in the case of Ahmed Sofa vs Hamid Box reported in 42 DLR 209 was cited in the context by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties where in the principle relied upon by him reads as under:-"Failure on the part of a judge to accept properly the submission of the learned Advocate resulting in an erroneous finding is no ground for review." 

23. This judgment concluded that "failure" to accept properly submissions of the Advocate cannot be a ground for review. We feel that the principle enunciated may be applied to the case we are dealing with at present. Since in the case before us also a similar circumstance exists as the one contemplated in the judgment in 42 DLR that we have referred to given that in this review application also the basic contention of the petitioners is that the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 "failed" to accept properly the submissions of the Advocate and which resulted in an erroneous finding. We are inclined to agree with this decision that failure to properly accept submissions cannot be a proper ground of review under Order XLVII of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

24. Besides, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties also took us to a decision of our Apex Court in the Case of Fazle Karim vs Bangladesh reported in 48 DLR (AD) 179 where the grounds in Order XLVII, rule 1 of the. Code of Civil Procedure was discussed and the Court placing its reliance upon Order XLVII concluded in para 7 of the judgment :-"The Rules provide that review of a judgment or order in a civil proceeding may be made "on grounds similar to those mentioned in Order XLVII, rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure" that is to say, on discovery of new and important matter or evidence which was not none or could not be produced before, (ii) on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or (iii) for any other sufficient reason. Consistently with the principle that there is to be an end to litigation, it is now well-recognised that review is not an appeal nor a rehearing merely on the ground that one party or another conceives himself to be dissatisfied with the decision sought to be reviewed. Unless a prayer for review is based on the grounds mentioned above, the Court will not sit on the .matter again for a fehearing or further hearing which is already concluded by decision even if that be erroneous." 

25. In another Para of the judgment in the same case their Lordships finding was—"No mistake in a considered conclusion, whatever the extent of that mistake, can be a ground for the exercise of review jurisdiction. It is not because a conclusion is wrong but because something obvious has been overlooked, some important aspect of the matter has not been considered, that a review petition will lie. It is a remedy to be used only in exceptional circumstances." 26. While drawing upon its own conclusion and opinion our Apex Court in that case also placed its reliance in the case of Mohd Amir Khan vs Controller of Estate Duty PLD 1962 (SC) 335 = 13 DLR (SC) 105, part of which we feel significant to repeat hereunder :— 

"The indulgence by way of review may no doubt be granted to prevent irremediable injustice being done by a Court of last resort as where by some inadvertence and important statutory provision has escaped notice which, if it had been noticed, might materially have affected the judgment of the Court but in no case should a rehearing be allowed upon merits." 

27. The main reason that we also feel that this principle in the case reported in PLD 1962 and which was relied upon by our Apex Court in the case of Fazle Karim vs Bangladesh is significant and applicable in this case is that a ground for review to be maintainable applies to a situation where something obvious has escaped notice or 'overlooked through inadvertence or any other reason whatsoever. But the case in hand does not reveal any such inadvertence or error. 

28. As we also discussed elsewhere in the judgment in this particular case there exists no such incident of having escaped notice of the 'overlooking' of any particular point or issue. Rather, the specific assertion and submissions on the point of law was duly noted down in the judgment itself. It is only that while doing so the High Court Division decided not to address it, for whatever its reasons. 

29. While deciding discerning upon the question of maintainability of review when or not a review application may be entertained. We feel it necessary to distinguish and severe between two situations. A situation where a specific point of law was raised, but the Court failed to take due notice of it and a situation where the Court did take notice, but consciously decided to refrain from addressing itself on the point raised. The first situation falls within the category of an inadvertent error or mistake and which is also apparent on the face of the record and in such case a review application may be maintainable. But our case here for reasons we already discussed comes within the scope of the second category and therefore in this case review application under Order XLVII the provisions of Order XLVII is not maintainable. 

30. We might safely conclude that in the case before us no 'overlooking' by any error or otherwise took place. Lastly the learned Advocate for the opposite parties drew our attention to another decision of our Apex Court in the case of Zenith Packages Limited vs Member Labour Appellate Tribunal Dhaka reported in 52 DLR (AD) 161 where the principle applicable to the present case reads as follows :-"Therefore on the grounds urged for review of judgment by the petitioner it seems to us that we are asked to sit over our judgment by way of appeal in a circuitous was addressing a lengthy and repeated submissions which already received our due notice in the judgment sought to be reviewed." 

31. From a close reading of the above and upon comparison of the circumstance in the case before us our considered finding is that, in this case submissions of the Counsel did duly receive notice of the Court and which is echoed in the judgment itself and therefore in respectful agreement with the principle set out by our Apex Court, we are of the opinion that we can-not sit upon our own judgment and embark upon a rehearing upon specific a point and therefore the only redress for the petitioner is such cases is the Appellate Forum and not Review. 

32. Our finding is that in the case we are dealing with at present the primary aspect which ought to be appreciated in the case, the fact of noting the submissions on a particular point of law in the judgment but yet making a conscious decision of restraining itself from addressing that point of law is discernible and thus distinguishable from a situation where a point was placed but was somehow overlooked or missed out by the Court by an inadvertent error. We therefore feel it necessary to reiterate that what is discernible here is that no such inadvertent "error" occurred in consequence of which Order XLVII, rule 1 could have come into play. Hence in this case the fact of noting the submissions in the judgment itself but yet consciously deciding not to dwell on the point makes all the difference and leaves no scope for a Review under the provision of Order XLVII of the Code. 
Application for review of judg-ment-1.(l) Any person considering himself aggrieved -(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred, (b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed, or (c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes, and who, from the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed or order made, or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree passed or order made against him, may apply for a review of judgment to the Court which passed the decree or made the order. 

(2) A party who is not appealing from a decree or order may apply for a review of judgment notwithstanding the pendency of an appeal by same other party except where the ground of such appeal is common to the applicant and the appellant, or when, being respondent, he can present to the Appellate Court the case on which he applies for the review. 2. An application for review of a decree or order of a Court, not being the High Court Division, upon some ground other than the discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or the existence of a clerical arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree, shall be made only to the judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to be reviewed; but any such application may, if the judge who passed the decree or made the order has ordered notice to issue under rule 4, sub-rule (2), proviso (a), be disposed of by his successor. 

33. Therefore upon hearing the learned Advocates from both sides and upon consideration of the decisions referred to and upon perusal of the judgment in First Appeal No. 177 of 1998 against which the instant review application was filed and taking the other materials on record and taking the facts and circumstances into consideration, it is our view that none of the grounds, mentioned in Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure against which a review may be maintainable in this particular case. Therefore, the only forum available to the petitioner could have been way by way of an Appeal before the appropriate forum. Hence we do find any substance in this Rule. 

In the result, the Rule as to Review is dis-charged without any order as to costs. 

Communicate the order at once. 

End.
